pronunciation-spelling.title_tr: Pronunciation and Spelling (ij, ui, the g sound)
pronunciation-spelling.intro_tr: Dutch spelling can look intimidating at first because it uses several vowel combinations that don't exist in English — ij, ui, ou/au, eu, oe — plus a guttural g/ch sound made at the back of the throat. The good news is that Dutch spelling is highly regular: almost every irregularity you'll meet (like why a plural suddenly gets a double letter, or why a "b" sounds like a "p") follows one core rule about open and closed syllables. Master the vowel sounds in the tables below, learn the open/closed syllable rule by heart, and the rest of Dutch spelling will start to make sense on its own. Note: the exact pronunciation of "g"/"ch" varies by region — Northern Dutch is harsher and more guttural, while Belgian/Southern Dutch is softer and more breathy; both are correct.

de-het-articles.intro_tr: Every Dutch noun belongs to one of two grammatical genders, and this gender decides which definite article ("the") it takes: "de" for common-gender nouns and "het" for neuter nouns. Roughly two-thirds of all Dutch nouns are de-woorden, while about one-third are het-woorden, and unfortunately the gender of a specific noun usually has to be memorized rather than derived from logic. Fortunately, several reliable patterns exist — for example, all plural nouns take "de" no matter what their singular form was, and all diminutives (-je words) always take "het". The indefinite article "een" (a/an) is identical for both genders, so it never reveals which definite article a noun needs — you must learn each noun as "de noun" or "het noun" from the start. This gender choice also has knock-on effects elsewhere in the grammar, most importantly for adjective endings (the -e suffix) and for how compound nouns get their gender.

plural-forms.intro_tr: Dutch nouns form their plural in two main ways: adding -en (the default, most common ending) or adding -s (used after certain word endings and vowel-final words). The choice between -en and -s is largely predictable from how the singular noun ends, but adding -en often triggers spelling adjustments — doubling a consonant or a vowel, or voicing a final f/s to v/z — to keep the vowel length correct. A set of very frequent nouns have irregular plurals, including an old-fashioned -eren ending (kind → kinderen) and internal vowel changes (stad → steden). Loanwords from Latin, Greek and other languages sometimes keep a foreign plural pattern alongside a regular Dutch one. This page collects the full rule set, the spelling changes, and the key exception lists you need to pluralize any Dutch noun with confidence.

personal-pronouns.intro_tr: Dutch personal pronouns change form depending on their grammatical role (subject vs. object) and whether they are stressed or unstressed in the sentence — a feature English doesn't have in the same way. Every pronoun (except 'u' and 'het') has a full/stressed form and a shortened/unstressed form, and choosing the wrong one is one of the most common beginner mistakes. Dutch also has a formality distinction ('jij/je' vs. 'u') similar to French tu/vous, and a special split in the 3rd person plural object form ('hen' vs. 'hun') that even many native speakers find tricky. Additionally, referring back to a noun requires knowing whether it's a 'de-woord' or 'het-woord', since this determines whether you use 'hij/hem', 'zij/ze', or 'het'. This page gives you the full pronoun paradigm plus the usage rules you'll need at every level.

present-tense.intro_tr: The Dutch present tense (tegenwoordige tijd) is the verb form you will use constantly from day one: for actions happening right now, habits, general truths, and even the near future when a time word makes things clear. Regular verbs are built by adding endings to the verb stem (infinitive minus -en), but several spelling rules — vowel doubling, v/z→f/s, and avoiding doubled t/d — change how that stem is actually written. A small set of extremely frequent verbs (zijn, hebben, gaan, doen, staan, weten) are irregular and simply have to be memorized. Finally, the conjugated verb always sits in second position in a Dutch main clause (the V2 rule), and the jij/je ending -t is dropped whenever jij/je comes right after the verb (as in questions).

zijn-hebben.intro_tr: Zijn (to be) and hebben (to have) are the two most important verbs in Dutch: they function as full verbs on their own (expressing states and possession) and as auxiliary verbs to build the perfect and past perfect tenses. Both are highly irregular and must be memorized as whole conjugation tables — there is no regular pattern to derive their forms from the infinitive. Choosing the correct auxiliary (zijn vs. hebben) for the perfect tense is one of the trickiest points for English speakers, since English only uses "have" for this purpose. This page gives you the full present-tense and past-tense conjugations, the rules for auxiliary selection, and a list of common exceptions to memorize.

word-order-v2.intro_tr: Dutch main clauses obey the "verb-second" (V2) rule: no matter which element opens the sentence, the finite (conjugated) verb must always sit in the second position of the clause. If something other than the subject — a time word, a place phrase, an object, an adverb, or even a whole subordinate clause — is moved to the front for emphasis, the subject simply jumps to the position right after the verb (this is called "inversion"). This is fundamentally different from English, where the subject stays glued before the verb regardless of what is fronted. V2 only applies to main clauses; subordinate clauses (after conjunctions like "omdat", "als", "dat") push the finite verb to the very end instead. Mastering V2 is the key that also unlocks separable verbs, question formation, and the main/subordinate clause split.

tables.caption_tr: The V2 Skeleton: what always sits where in a Dutch main clause
footnotes_tr: No matter what fills position 1, the finite verb never moves from position 2 — this is the defining rule of Dutch main-clause word order.
Position 1 can only ever hold ONE grammatical unit, even if that unit is a long phrase or an entire subordinate clause.

tables.caption_tr: What kind of element can occupy position 1 (and trigger inversion)
rows: I am going to Paris tomorrow.
Tomorrow I am going to Paris.
Die film heb ik al gezien.
I have already seen that movie.
Aan haar geef ik het cadeau.
I give the present to her.
Omdat het regent, blijf ik thuis.
Because it's raining, I'm staying home.
Er staat een man voor de deur.
There is a man standing at the door.
footnotes_tr: Whatever is fronted receives contrastive or topical emphasis — this is a major tool for controlling focus in Dutch, unlike fixed-order English.

tables.caption_tr: V2 plus verb clusters: the finite verb stays in P2, everything else goes to the end
footnotes_tr: Only the FINITE (conjugated) verb form takes position 2; infinitives, past participles, and separable prefixes are always pushed to the very end of the main clause.

tables.caption_tr: Main clause (V2) vs. subordinate clause (verb-final) — the crucial contrast
rows: Element-1 + FINITE VERB + subject (if not P1) + rest
'Ik denk' is a main clause: verb 'denk' is in position 2.
Subordinate clause (after dat, omdat, als, etc.)
Inside 'dat hij komt', the verb 'komt' is pushed to clause-final position — NOT V2.
Subordinate clause fronted as P1 of the main clause
[Whole subordinate clause] + MAIN VERB + subject + rest
Als het regent, blijven we thuis.
The entire 'Als het regent' clause fills main-clause position 1; 'blijven' is still position 2 of the main clause.
Ik kook, en jij dekt de tafel.
Coordinating conjunctions (en, maar, want, of, dus) do NOT affect word order — both sides stay V2.
footnotes_tr: This main-vs-subordinate split is one of the most important structural facts in Dutch grammar and explains many word-order 'exceptions' students encounter.

tables.caption_tr: Verb position in different sentence types: statements, wh-questions, and yes/no questions
rows: Verb = position 1 (no fronted element at all)
footnotes_tr: Yes/no questions and imperatives are 'V1' (verb-first) — they are the main exceptions to the V2 rule, not violations of it, since there is simply nothing in position 1.

tables.caption_tr: Common word-order mistakes English speakers make
rows: Subject 'ik' wrongly kept before the verb after fronting 'vandaag'; verb must stay in position 2.
Ik heb gisteren gegeten een pizza.
Past participle 'gegeten' placed mid-sentence instead of at the very end of the clause.
Ik heb gisteren een pizza gegeten.
Ik denk dat hij komt morgen.
Finite verb 'komt' should be pushed to the end of the subordinate clause, not stay after the subject.
Ik denk dat hij morgen komt.
Omdat het regent ik blijf thuis.
After a fronted subordinate clause, the main clause still needs inversion (verb before subject).
Omdat het regent, blijf ik thuis.
In a wh-question the finite verb must directly follow the question word (position 2), not the subject.

examples.translation_tr: I am reading a book. (subject in position 1, verb in position 2 — normal order)

examples.target: Vandaag lees ik een boek.
examples.translation_tr: Today I am reading a book. (time expression takes position 1, so subject 'ik' and verb swap places — inversion)

examples.target: In Amsterdam woont mijn zus.
examples.translation_tr: My sister lives in Amsterdam. (place phrase fronted, verb stays second, subject moves after the verb)

examples.target: Dit boek heb ik al gelezen.
examples.translation_tr: I have already read this book. (object fronted for emphasis; finite verb 'heb' stays second, participle 'gelezen' goes to the very end)

examples.target: Morgen ga ik met de trein naar Utrecht.
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow I'm going to Utrecht by train. (time adverb in position 1 forces inversion of subject and verb)

examples.target: Helaas kan ik morgen niet komen.
examples.translation_tr: Unfortunately I can't come tomorrow. (adverb 'helaas' fronted; modal verb 'kan' is the finite verb-2, infinitive 'komen' goes to the end)

examples.target: Als het regent, blijven we thuis.
examples.translation_tr: If it rains, we stay home. (the whole subordinate clause 'Als het regent' counts as ONE position-1 slot, so the main clause verb 'blijven' still comes second)

examples.target: Waarom kom je niet naar het feest?
examples.translation_tr: Why aren't you coming to the party? (wh-question: question word is position 1, finite verb 'kom' is position 2 — still V2, unlike yes/no questions)

negation-niet-geen.intro_tr: Dutch has two main negation words, and choosing the right one is one of the first real grammar challenges for beginners: 'geen' negates an indefinite noun (replacing 'een' or an implied 'some/any'), while 'niet' negates almost everything else — definite nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositional phrases, and whole clauses. Unlike English 'not', Dutch 'niet' does not always sit next to the verb; its position shifts depending on what exactly is being negated, following fairly predictable placement rules. 'geen' itself never changes form — it works for masculine, feminine, neuter, and plural nouns alike. Mastering the geen/niet split plus the placement rules for 'niet' is essential before moving on to more advanced negation words like 'nauwelijks' or 'evenmin'.

tables.caption_tr: Core Rule: geen vs. niet
rows: an indefinite noun (singular or plural; where English would use 'a/an', 'some', 'any', or no article at all)
Ik heb geen fiets. (I don't have a bike.)
everything else: definite nouns (de/het/possessive/demonstrative + noun), proper names, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositional phrases, whole clauses
niet + [the element being negated], or niet at clause end
Ik heb de fiets niet. (I don't have the bike.)
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: if the affirmative sentence would use 'een' or no article before the noun, the negative uses 'geen'. If the affirmative uses 'de/het', 'mijn', 'dit/dat', etc., the negative uses 'niet'.

tables.caption_tr: geen: Form and Agreement
rows: 'geen' never changes for gender (de/het) or number (singular/plural)
geen man / geen vrouw / geen kind / geen mannen
In the affirmative 'een auto' → negative 'geen auto' (the article 'een' disappears entirely)
Ik heb een auto. → Ik heb geen auto.
No article in the affirmative → 'geen' in the negative
Ik drink koffie. → Ik drink geen koffie.
'geen' cannot combine with de/het, mijn, dit/dat — use 'niet' instead
Ik zie de hond niet. (NOT: Ik zie geen de hond.)
Ik heb geen twee euro. (I don't even have two euros.)

tables.caption_tr: Position Rules for niet
rows: If there is no specific complement to negate, 'niet' goes to the very end of the clause (before any final verb cluster)
Ik ken hem niet. / Ik heb hem niet gezien.
When negating a specific adjective, adverb, or prepositional phrase, 'niet' is placed directly before it
Hij is niet groot. / Ik werk niet snel. / Zij komt niet uit Utrecht.
A definite noun phrase (de/het/mijn + noun) stays before 'niet'
Before an indefinite direct object → use geen instead
Do not use 'niet' + indefinite noun; switch to 'geen'
Ik lees geen boek. (NOT: Ik lees een boek niet.)
'niet' precedes the separated prefix at the end of the clause
Ik bel je niet op. / Ik ruim mijn kamer niet op.
Before past participles / infinitives at clause end
In perfect tense or with modal verbs, 'niet' comes right before the final verb form(s)
Ik heb het niet gedaan. / Ik wil dat niet doen.
Time adverbials (vandaag, gisteren, om 3 uur) usually precede 'niet'
Ik kom vandaag niet. / Ze belt morgen niet.
Time – Manner – Place, niet before Place
In the standard TMP order, 'niet' typically sits after time/manner but before a place phrase
Ik ga vanavond niet naar de bioscoop.

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Combinations
rows: no longer / not anymore (negating a verb/action)
Ik rook niet meer. (I no longer smoke.)
no more ... left (negating a noun quantity)
Ik heb geen brood meer. (I have no more bread.)
not at all / no ... at all
Dat vind ik helemaal niet leuk.
Het kost niet meer dan tien euro.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: geen vs. niet
rows: Indefinite noun 'een auto' must become 'geen auto', not 'een auto niet'.
'geen' cannot be combined with the definite article 'de'.
Profession/role nouns after 'zijn' follow the indefinite-noun rule → 'geen'.
Ik hou niet van koffie niet.
Only one negation word is needed; Dutch does not double negatives like some other languages.
Time expressions normally precede 'niet' rather than following it directly after the verb.

examples.target: Ik heb geen tijd.
examples.translation_tr: I don't have (any) time.
examples.note_tr: 'geen' negates the indefinite noun 'tijd' (no article needed).

examples.target: Ik zie het boek niet.
examples.translation_tr: I don't see the book.
examples.note_tr: 'niet' is used because 'het boek' is a definite noun phrase; it stands right before it isn't required here since it comes after the object.

examples.target: Zij is niet moe.
examples.translation_tr: She is not tired.
examples.note_tr: 'niet' directly precedes the adjective it negates.

examples.target: Hij drinkt geen koffie.
examples.translation_tr: He doesn't drink coffee.
examples.note_tr: Uncountable/indefinite noun 'koffie' → 'geen'.

examples.target: Ik ga niet naar het feest.
examples.translation_tr: I'm not going to the party.
examples.note_tr: 'niet' comes before the prepositional phrase of place 'naar het feest'.

examples.target: Wij hebben geen kinderen.
examples.translation_tr: We don't have (any) children.
examples.note_tr: Plural indefinite noun → 'geen', invariable for number/gender.

examples.target: Ik heb geen geld meer.
examples.translation_tr: I don't have any money anymore / I'm out of money.
examples.note_tr: Fixed combination 'geen ... meer' = 'no more/none left'.

examples.target: Ik hou ook niet van vis.
examples.translation_tr: I don't like fish either.
examples.note_tr: 'ook niet' = 'not... either'; 'niet' sits right before the prepositional phrase 'van vis'.

question-formation.intro_tr: Dutch questions come in two basic types: yes/no questions and wh-questions (open questions with a question word), and both rely on the same core trick — putting the finite verb before the subject (inversion), the mirror image of normal statement order. There is no equivalent of English "do-support," so you never say "Doe jij werken?" — you simply invert the verb you already have: "Werk je?". Question words (wie, wat, waar, wanneer, hoe, waarom, welke/welk) sit in the very first position, immediately followed by the inverted verb and then the subject. A special quirk to memorize early: when the subject "jij/je" comes right after the verb, the verb drops its final -t (Jij werkt → Werk jij?), but this does not happen with the polite "u". Separable verb prefixes still jump to the very end of the question, exactly as in statements.

tables.caption_tr: Question Words (Wh-Words)
rows: how come / what do you mean

tables.caption_tr: Yes/No Questions: Inversion Across All Persons
rows: Do you live in Utrecht? (verb drops -t before jij)
Do you live in Utrecht? (formal — keeps -t)
footnotes_tr: Rule: when 'jij/je' is placed directly after the verb, the verb loses its final -t: 'Jij werkt' -> 'Werk jij?'. This 'jij-drop' rule never applies to 'u' or to any other subject.

tables.caption_tr: Wh-Question Formation Pattern
rows: What is your name? (formal, lit. 'how are you called')
footnotes_tr: Pattern: [Question word] + [finite verb] + [subject] + [rest of the sentence] + ?

tables.caption_tr: Questions with Modal Verbs
rows: Kun je dit voor me doen?
Can you do this for me?
Do I have to go already?
Do you want something to drink?
footnotes_tr: Only the modal verb inverts with the subject; any second (infinitive) verb still goes to the end of the sentence, just as in statements.

tables.caption_tr: Questions with Separable Verbs
rows: Are you getting up early tomorrow?
Hij komt om acht uur aan.
Komt hij om acht uur aan?
Does he arrive at eight o'clock?
footnotes_tr: The separable prefix (op, aan, mee, etc.) always stays at the very end of the question, even though the main verb has moved to the front.

tables.caption_tr: welk vs. welke vs. wat voor (een)
rows: any noun; asks about type/kind rather than a specific item
What kind of car do you have?
footnotes_tr: 'een' after 'wat voor' is optional and often dropped in speech: 'Wat voor auto...' and 'Wat voor een auto...' are both correct.

tables.caption_tr: Asking About Things with a Preposition: waar + Preposition
footnotes_tr: Use 'waar' + preposition only when asking about a thing/idea. For people, use preposition + 'wie' instead: 'Met wie ga je?' (Who are you going with?), never 'waarmee' for a person.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes in Question Formation
rows: Dutch has no do-support; simply invert the verb you already have.
The -t is dropped only before 'jij/je', never before 'u'.
Wat voor een auto is dit voor?
Wat voor auto is dit? / Waarvoor is dit?
Avoid stacking two prepositional question forms in one sentence.
Met wat ga je naar het feest?
Met wie ga je naar het feest?
For people use 'wie' with a preposition, not a 'waar-' combination.
The verb must directly follow the question word; the subject comes after the verb.

examples.translation_tr: Do you work here?
examples.note_tr: Yes/no question: verb comes before the subject (inversion).

examples.target: Waar woon jij?
examples.translation_tr: Where do you live?
examples.note_tr: Wh-question: question word + verb + subject.

examples.target: Kun je me helpen?
examples.translation_tr: Can you help me?
examples.note_tr: Modal verb 'kunnen' inverted with subject 'je'.

examples.target: Bel je me morgen op?
examples.translation_tr: Will you call me tomorrow?
examples.note_tr: Separable verb 'opbellen': the prefix 'op' stays at the very end.

examples.target: Wat voor auto heb je?
examples.translation_tr: What kind of car do you have?
examples.note_tr: 'wat voor (een)' asks about type/kind, regardless of de/het.

examples.target: Welke trein neem je?
examples.translation_tr: Which train do you take?
examples.note_tr: 'welke' is used because 'trein' is a de-word.

examples.target: Waarover praten jullie?
examples.translation_tr: What are you (pl.) talking about?
examples.note_tr: 'waar' + preposition replaces 'over wat' when asking about a thing.

examples.target: Ga je niet mee?
examples.translation_tr: Aren't you coming along?
examples.note_tr: Negative yes/no question: 'niet' still follows the same inversion pattern.

numbers-time.intro_tr: Dutch cardinal numbers above twenty are built unit-before-ten (eenentwintig = "one-and-twenty" = 21), the reverse of English word order, and are written as a single word. Ordinal numbers are formed by adding -de or -ste to the cardinal, with a handful of irregular forms to memorize. Telling time in everyday Dutch revolves around the half hour rather than the hour: "half vier" means 3:30 (halfway TO four), which is the single biggest trap for English speakers. Alongside this colloquial clock system, Dutch also uses an official 24-hour format (without kwart/half) for timetables, TV schedules, and formal announcements. This page collects the full number system, ordinal formation, and every clock-time pattern in one place.

tables.caption_tr: Cardinal Numbers 0–20
rows: 'één' with accents when counting/emphasizing, to distinguish from the article 'een' (a/an)

tables.caption_tr: Tens and Compound Numbers (20–100)
rows: unit + en + ten, one word: een-en-twintig
diaeresis (ë) added to keep vowels separate: twee-ën-dertig

tables.caption_tr: Large Numbers and Number Formatting
rows: period (.) marks thousands, not a comma
comma (,) marks the decimal point — opposite of English
prices: whole euros + cents, no 'komma' needed

tables.caption_tr: Ordinal Numbers (1st–20th) and Formation Rule
rows: irregular — takes -ste, not -de (acht already ends in a 't'-like sound)

tables.caption_tr: Telling Time: the Half-Hour System (example hour 3:00–4:00)
footnotes_tr: The Dutch clock always looks FORWARD to the next hour once past :15 — 'half vier' is 3:30, and everything between 3:15 and 4:00 is expressed relative to 'half vier' or 'vier', never relative to 'drie'.
In casual speech 'uur' is often dropped after exact hours in context, e.g. 'Ik kom om drie' (I'll come at three).

rows: What time does the movie start?

rows: twaalf gedeeld door drie is vier (12÷3=4)
used in both spoken and written sums

adjective-inflection.intro_tr: In Dutch, an adjective placed directly in front of a noun (the "attributive" position) usually adds an -e ending — this is called adjective inflection. De-words always take this -e, in the singular and the plural, no matter which article is used. Het-words are the tricky case: in the plural they also take -e, but in the singular they only take -e after a definite determiner (het, dit, dat, or a possessive); after een, geen, or no article at all, the adjective stays in its bare dictionary form. Adjectives used predicatively (after zijn, worden, lijken, blijven) never take -e, and a closed set of adjectives (materials in -en, some loanwords, quantity words) are always invariable. A few adjectives also undergo a spelling change (like a doubled consonant or a dropped vowel) when the -e is added.

tables.caption_tr: The Basic Rule: When to Add -e
rows: de grote hond / een grote hond / grote honden
het grote huis / dit grote huis / mijn grote huis
een groot huis / geen groot huis

tables.caption_tr: Determiners That Block -e Before a Singular het-word
footnotes_tr: This rule only applies to SINGULAR het-words. In the plural, or with de-words, the adjective always takes -e regardless of which determiner is used.

tables.caption_tr: Spelling Changes When Adding -e
rows: double the final consonant to keep the vowel short
drop one vowel letter (syllable becomes open)

tables.caption_tr: Adjectives That Never Add -e (Invariable)
rows: Already end in -en (materials & a few others)
houten, gouden, zilveren, stalen, wollen, glazen, katoenen, open, eigen
Identical form everywhere: een houten tafel / de houten tafel / houten tafels
roze, oranje, lila, beige, paars (informal variation)
No extra -e is added; the spoken/written form does not change
Normally stay uninflected: veel mensen, weinig tijd, genoeg geld

tables.caption_tr: Predicative vs. Attributive Position
rows: een grote hond / het grote huis / grote honden
Predicative (after zijn, worden, lijken, blijven, schijnen)
Adjective NEVER takes -e; stays in base form
De hond is groot. / Het huis lijkt groot. / De honden worden groot.

tables.caption_tr: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives Follow the Same Rule
rows: een mooiere auto / het mooiere huis / mooiere auto's
de mooiste auto / het mooiste huis / de mooiste auto's
footnotes_tr: The comparative -er form takes -e exactly like a normal adjective (subject to the het-word/een exception). The superlative -ste form already ends in -e, so no further change is possible.

modal-verbs.title_tr: Modal Verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, hoeven, zullen)
modal-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, hoeven, zullen) express ability, obligation, desire, permission, necessity, and future/suggestion, and they behave like their English counterparts by combining with a bare infinitive that goes to the end of the clause. Their present-tense conjugation is irregular and does not follow the normal -t rule for the jij/u forms with several of them (kan/kunt, wil/wilt), so these forms must be memorized. A key trap for beginners is the difference between "moeten niet" (should not, discouraged) and "niet hoeven" (don't need to, no obligation) — mixing these up completely changes the meaning. In the perfect and past-perfect tenses, modal verbs trigger the famous "double infinitive" construction, where the modal appears in its infinitive form instead of as a past participle. Mastering these six verbs is essential since they appear in almost every conversation at A1 level and beyond.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: the six modal verbs and their core meanings
rows: physical/mental capability or possibility that something can happen
internal or external necessity, often stronger than 'should'
expresses what the subject wants; 'zou willen' = 'would like'
asking or granting permission; also used for polite requests
almost always combined with niet/geen; requires 'te' before infinitive (unlike the other modals)
don't need to, don't have to
used for the future tense and for polite offers/suggestions ('Zal ik...?')

tables.caption_tr: Present tense (tegenwoordige tijd) — full conjugation
footnotes_tr: 'kun je?' (instead of 'kan je?') is common in questions, both are accepted in speech.
'wilt' is the more formal/written jij-form; 'wil' is common in speech.
'u' always takes the formal 2nd-person form: kunt, wilt, zult (never kan/wil/zal with u in careful writing).

tables.caption_tr: Past tense (onvoltooid verleden tijd) — full conjugation
footnotes_tr: 'wou' is an informal alternative to 'wilde', very common in speech.
'zou/zouden' is the base of the Dutch conditional mood and is used constantly outside of pure past-tense contexts (e.g. 'Ik zou graag...' = 'I would like...').

tables.caption_tr: Critical negation nuances: don't confuse these!
rows: should not / must not (discouraged, sometimes prohibited)
don't need to / no obligation at all
Je hoeft dat niet te doen.
You don't need to do that.
You're not allowed to do that.
same as above, word order variant
footnotes_tr: 'moeten niet' and 'niet hoeven' are the #1 confusion point for English speakers: 'must not' in English can wrongly be translated as 'moeten niet', but Dutch 'moeten niet' really means 'should not/had better not', while true absence of obligation is 'niet hoeven'.

tables.caption_tr: Word order with modal verbs
rows: modal + ... + separable verb stays together as infinitive at the end
I have to turn on the light.
...dat + subject + ... + modal + infinitive (both verbs cluster at the very end)
Ik weet dat hij morgen moet werken.
I know that he has to work tomorrow.
hebben/zijn + ... + infinitive + modal (both in infinitive form, modal last)
I have had to work. / I had to work.
...dat + subject + hebben/zijn + infinitive + modal (all verbs at the end, hebben/zijn first)
footnotes_tr: This 'double infinitive' (dubbele infinitief) is unique to modal verbs and a few others like laten/zien/horen: the modal never becomes a past participle (never 'gemoeten', 'gekund' in this construction) when combined with another infinitive.

rows: Word order/register error; sounds blunt as a request
Ik wil graag koffie. / Mag ik een kopje koffie? (more polite)
Je moet niet komen, meaning 'you don't have to come'
hoeven requires 'te' before the infinitive, unlike the other modals
Kan je alsjeblieft...? (as very formal request)
grammatically fine but 'kun je' or 'zou je kunnen' sounds more natural/polite
zullen is also used constantly for offers/suggestions, not just future tense
Zal ik dat voor je doen? (Shall I do that for you?)

examples.translation_tr: I can swim well.
examples.note_tr: kunnen = ability/possibility

examples.translation_tr: You must read this book.
examples.note_tr: moeten = obligation/necessity

examples.note_tr: willen = desire/want

separable-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch has a large group of verbs built from a prefix + a base verb, called separable verbs (scheidbare werkwoorden). In most finite clause types the prefix breaks off and jumps to the very end of the clause, while the stress always falls on the prefix itself (OPbellen, not opBELlen). This splitting happens in the present and past simple tenses and in main clauses; in subordinate clauses, with modal verbs, and in te-infinitive constructions, the prefix instead stays attached to the verb (though word order differs in each case). In the perfect tense, ge- is inserted between the prefix and the stem (op·ge·beld). Because the meaning of a separable verb is often completely different from its base verb (bellen "to ring" vs. opbellen "to call"), and because a handful of prefixes can be either separable or inseparable with different meanings, this topic needs careful attention and constant reference.

perfect-tense.intro_tr: The perfectum (perfect tense) is by far the most common way Dutch speakers talk about the past in everyday conversation — much more frequent than the simple past (imperfectum). It is a compound tense: a present-tense auxiliary (hebben "to have" or zijn "to be") is combined with a past participle, which is normally pushed to the very end of the clause. Choosing the right auxiliary and forming the past participle correctly (regular vs. irregular, with or without ge-) are the two main challenges for learners. This page gives you the full formation rules, the complete list of high-frequency irregular participles, and the word-order patterns you need.

imperfect-tense.intro_tr: The imperfectum (simple past) is Dutch's main narrative past tense, used for habitual, ongoing, or sequential past actions and often paired with time expressions like gisteren, vroeger, or toen. Regular ("weak") verbs form the imperfectum by adding -te(n) or -de(n) to the stem, with the choice determined by the final consonant of the stem (the famous 't kofschip rule). Irregular ("strong") verbs instead change their stem vowel and take no -t/-d ending; these must be memorized individually, similar to English strong verbs (sing–sang). Unlike the perfectum, which dominates spoken conversation, the imperfectum is essential in writing, storytelling, and for verbs like zijn, hebben, and the modal verbs, which almost always appear in imperfectum form even in speech. Mastering this tense requires learning the 't kofschip rule for weak verbs and building up a personal list of common strong verb stem changes.

subordinate-clauses.intro_tr: Dutch subordinate clauses (bijzinnen) are introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as omdat, dat, als, and terwijl. Unlike main clauses, where the finite verb must occupy the second position, a subordinate clause pushes ALL verbs — finite verbs, modals, auxiliaries, and separable prefixes — to the very end of the clause. This is one of the most distinctive features of Dutch word order and a frequent source of mistakes for English speakers. When a subordinate clause is placed at the beginning of a sentence, the following main clause still obeys the V2 rule, so the subject and finite verb invert. Mastering this verb-final pattern is essential for producing natural, correct Dutch sentences.

er-usage.intro_tr: Dutch "er" is a small word with several distinct jobs, and beginners mainly need to master its most frequent role: introducing an indefinite subject in existential sentences ("er is / er zijn" = "there is / there are"). Beyond that, "er" can also stand in, unstressed, for a place already mentioned (instead of repeating "daar"), and it appears before bare numbers or quantity words when referring back to something already named ("Ik heb er twee" = "I have two of them"). "Er" can also combine with prepositions (erover, ermee, eraan) to refer to things rather than people — this basic pattern is expanded in a later, more advanced lesson. A key rule to memorize early: whenever the real subject of a Dutch sentence is indefinite and it doesn't occupy the first position, "er" fills that first slot instead.

comparatives.intro_tr: Dutch adjectives form the comparative by adding -er and the superlative by adding -st to the base (positive) form, much like English "-er/-est" but used far more consistently, even with long adjectives. A handful of very common adjectives are irregular (goed→beter→best), and a small set of spelling rules (consonant doubling, vowel-length changes, -r/-s/-f endings) affect how the suffix attaches. Comparisons are expressed with dan ("than") for inequality and (net) zo... als / even... als for equality, while the superlative always appears with an article (de/het) and takes the usual attributive -e ending, but drops it in predicative position. A special "the more..., the more..." pattern uses hoe + comparative twice, and a periphrastic form with meer/meest replaces the suffix for participles and certain adjective types.

future-tense.intro_tr: Dutch has no dedicated future-tense verb ending; instead, three overlapping strategies express future meaning. The present tense alone can signal a near, scheduled event when a time word is present (Ik vertrek morgen — I leave tomorrow). The construction gaan + infinitive, much like English "going to," is used for plans, intentions, and things already set in motion. The construction zullen + infinitive, much like English "will," is used for predictions, promises, offers, and spontaneous decisions. Both gaan and zullen are irregular, extremely common verbs that must be memorized fully, and in a main clause the conjugated verb (gaan or zullen) sits in second position while the accompanying infinitive is pushed all the way to the end of the clause. Zullen also has a very frequent non-future use, expressing probability or assumption about the present (Hij zal wel moe zijn — He's probably tired).

diminutives.intro_tr: Dutch diminutives are formed by adding a suffix (mainly -je, with several spelling-based variants) to a noun to indicate smallness, affection, informality, or a completely new lexicalized meaning. The exact suffix (-je, -pje, -tje, -etje, or -kje) depends on the final sound of the noun, and some words also change their spelling (vowel lengthening or consonant doubling) when the ending is added. Every diminutive, regardless of the gender of the original noun, becomes a "het"-word, and its plural is always formed with -s. Diminutives are extremely common in everyday spoken Dutch, so mastering the suffix rules and their pragmatic uses (not just literal smallness) is essential.

tables.caption_tr: Main rules for choosing the diminutive suffix

the final vowel is doubled in spelling
auto → autootje; foto → fotootje; paraplu → parapluutje
A diphthong at the end (ei/ij, ui, ooi, aai, oei, eeuw, ieuw, uw...)
ei → eitje; kooi → kooitje; leeuw → leeuwtje
-l, -n, -r, -w after a LONG vowel or diphthong
deur → deurtje; trein → treintje; zoon → zoontje
man → mannetje; bal → balletje; kam → kammetje; kar → karretje

reflexive-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch reflexive verbs (wederkerende werkwoorden) describe an action the subject performs on or for itself, so they require a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject in person and number. Some verbs are only ever reflexive (like zich vergissen - to be mistaken), while many ordinary verbs become reflexive with a shift in meaning (wassen "to wash something" vs. zich wassen "to wash oneself"). Unlike English, Dutch has two sets of reflexive forms: the short unstressed forms (me, je, zich, ons) used in normal sentences, and the emphatic -zelf compounds (mezelf, jezelf, zichzelf...) used for contrast, emphasis, or after prepositions. The reflexive pronoun's position in the sentence follows the same word-order rules as other object pronouns, so it can appear in different spots depending on main clause, question, subordinate clause, or perfect tense structure. Mastering the pronoun table and the list of common reflexive verbs is essential, since many high-frequency daily verbs (getting dressed, feeling, hurrying, remembering) are reflexive in Dutch even when their English equivalent is not.

passive-voice.intro_tr: Dutch forms the passive voice with the verb "worden" (literally "to become") plus the past participle, used for actions and processes ("De auto wordt gewassen" = The car is being washed). This contrasts with English, which uses only "to be" for both an ongoing action and a resulting state — Dutch instead uses "worden" for the action (dynamic passive) and "zijn" for the state that results from it (stative passive). The agent who performs the action, if mentioned, is introduced with "door" (by), not "van". In compound tenses, "worden" itself is conjugated (word, wordt, werd, is/was + participle, without the expected "geworden"), while the past participle of the main verb stays fixed. In subordinate clauses and with modal verbs, "worden" behaves like any other verb and moves to the end of the clause as part of the verb cluster.

conditional.intro_tr: Dutch conditional sentences link a condition (introduced by "als" = if) with a result clause, and the verb "zou/zouden" (would) marks hypothetical or unreal situations, much like English "would". There are three basic types: real/open conditions (present + present), present unreal conditions (simple past + zou + infinitive), and past unreal conditions (past perfect + zou + hebben/zijn + past participle). Word order is crucial: when the "als"-clause comes first, it counts as the first position of the sentence, so the main clause must start with the verb (often followed by "dan"); when the main clause comes first, normal order applies and "dan" is dropped. In more formal or literary Dutch, "als" can even be omitted entirely, with the condition expressed through subject-verb inversion instead.

tables.caption_tr: The three types of conditional sentences
rows: A realistic, possible condition, often a general rule or a real future possibility
Als het regent, blijf ik thuis. (If it rains, I stay home.)
An imagined situation that is not true now, contrary to present reality
Als ik rijk was, zou ik reizen. (If I were rich, I would travel.)
An imagined situation in the past that did not actually happen
Als ik het geweten had, zou ik gekomen zijn. (If I had known, I would have come.)
footnotes_tr: Even though the als-clause uses a past tense form in types 2 and 3, the meaning is not about the past — it signals unreality, not time (compare English 'If I were...').
Past unreal conditions ('zou hebben gedaan') are covered in more depth in the separate Past Conditional topic.

Zou jij dat doen? (Would you do that?)
Hij zou blij zijn. (He would be happy.)
Wij zouden graag komen. (We would like to come.)
Zouden jullie meehelpen? (Would you [pl.] help out?)

footnotes_tr: 'Zou/zouden' is historically the simple past of 'zullen', but in conditionals it functions purely as the equivalent of English 'would', not as a real past tense.
For past unreal conditions, add 'hebben' or 'zijn' + past participle: 'zou hebben gedaan', 'zou zijn gegaan'.

tables.caption_tr: Word order: als-clause first vs. main clause first
rows: Als ik geld had, (dan) zou ik een auto kopen.
Ik zou een auto kopen als ik geld had.
Had ik geld, dan zou ik een auto kopen.
footnotes_tr: When the als-clause opens the sentence, it occupies the first position, forcing the main clause to start with the finite verb — this is the V2 rule applied to conditionals.
'Dan' (then) is optional but very common after a fronted als-clause; it is never used when the main clause comes first.

relative-clauses.intro_tr: A Dutch relative clause adds extra information about a noun that was just mentioned (the "antecedent"), similar to English "who/which/that/where" clauses. The choice between die, dat, and waar is not random: it depends on whether the antecedent is a de-word or het-word, whether it's singular or plural, and whether the clause needs a preposition. Just like in other subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb is pushed to the very end of the relative clause. A comma normally separates the relative clause from the rest of the sentence (unlike in English). Watch out: gender agreement is always grammatical, not natural — so "het meisje" (the girl) still takes "dat", not "die", even though it refers to a female person.

aan-het-progressive.title_tr: Continuous/Progressive Aspect: aan het + Infinitive, zitten/staan te
aan-het-progressive.intro_tr: Dutch has two common periphrastic constructions to express that an action is ongoing, similar to the English "-ing" progressive form. The most neutral and widely used one is "aan het + infinitive", combined with a conjugated form of zijn (to be). The second option uses a posture verb — zitten (to sit), staan (to stand), liggen (to lie), or lopen (to walk) — followed by "te + infinitive"; this construction additionally describes the physical position or manner of the subject while performing the action. Neither construction is grammatically obligatory the way the English progressive is: Dutch simple present/past tenses can also express ongoing actions, so these forms are used specifically to emphasize that something is "in the middle of happening." Choosing between the two options depends mostly on register and whether the posture information is relevant or natural.

om-te-infinitive.intro_tr: The construction "om ... te + infinitive" is the Dutch counterpart of English "in order to" or simply "to" + infinitive, and it introduces a subordinate clause that expresses purpose/goal, or is grammatically required after many verbs, adjectives, and nouns. Unlike English, Dutch places "om" at the very front of the clause and "te + infinitive" at the very end, with any objects, adverbs, reflexive pronouns, or separable-verb prefixes sandwiched in between. When the infinitive clause simply completes the meaning of certain verbs (proberen, beginnen, weigeren, vergeten, hopen, durven, etc.) rather than expressing purpose, "om" is dropped and only bare "te + infinitive" is used. Getting the word order right — "om" first, "te + infinitive" last, everything else in the middle — is one of the biggest trouble spots for English speakers, since English usually places "to" immediately after the verb.

imperative-mood.intro_tr: The Dutch imperative mood is used to give commands, instructions, requests, suggestions, and warnings. In the vast majority of cases it is formed simply from the bare verb stem — the same form used for the 'ik' conjugation — without any subject pronoun attached. Unlike English, Dutch does not distinguish between singular and plural addressees in the informal imperative: the same stem form works whether you're speaking to one person or a whole group. A separate, more polite form exists for formally addressing someone with 'u', made by adding -t to the stem (often, but not always, followed by 'u' itself). A small number of very frequent verbs (zijn, hebben) have irregular imperative stems that simply have to be memorized, and particles like eens, even, maar, and toch are commonly added to soften or shape the tone of a command.

fixed-prepositions.title_tr: Fixed Prepositions with Verbs (wachten op, denken aan)
fixed-prepositions.intro_tr: Many Dutch verbs are permanently paired with a specific preposition that does not always match the preposition English uses for the same idea — these are called "vaste voorzetsels" (fixed prepositions). For example, "wachten" always pairs with "op" (not "voor", as English "wait for" might suggest), and "denken" pairs with "aan" when you mean "have someone/something in mind". Because the combination is fixed and often unpredictable from the English translation, these verb+preposition pairs simply have to be memorized as single vocabulary chunks. When asking about or referring back to the thing introduced by the fixed preposition, Dutch uses special question/pronoun forms: "waar-" compounds (waarop, waaraan...) for questions about things, and "er-/daar-" compounds (erop, eraan, daarop, daaraan...) to refer back to things already mentioned — but a plain preposition + personal pronoun (op hem, aan haar) when referring to people. Mastering this list is essential for natural-sounding, idiomatic Dutch at B1 level.

conjunctions.title_tr: Conjunctions: Main and Subordinate Clause Word Order (want vs omdat)
conjunctions.intro_tr: Dutch conjunctions split into two grammatical families that trigger completely different word order, and this is one of the biggest traps for English speakers. Coordinating conjunctions (en, maar, of, want, dus) simply glue two independent clauses together and leave normal main-clause word order intact (conjugated verb stays in 2nd position). Subordinating conjunctions (omdat, dat, als, terwijl, and many more) turn the following clause into a dependent clause and send the conjugated verb all the way to the end. The classic confusion pair is want vs omdat: both translate as "because", but want keeps the verb in place while omdat kicks it to the end. Mastering this switch is essential because in Dutch, verb position is one of the clearest grammatical signals a listener relies on.

pronominal-adverbs.intro_tr: Dutch never combines a preposition directly with the pronoun "het" or "dat" to refer back to a thing, idea, or previously mentioned non-human noun — you cannot say "op het" or "van het" meaning "on it / of it". Instead, Dutch fuses a special base word with the preposition into a single pronominal adverb: er- (unstressed, neutral reference), daar- (stressed, contrastive "that"), hier- (stressed, "this"), or waar- (question/relative "what, which"). This gives forms like erop ("on it"), ermee ("with it"), waarover ("about what/which"), daarnaar ("toward that"). Crucially, these forms are only used for things and ideas; when referring to people, ordinary preposition + pronoun (met hem, aan haar) is still required. In many clause types the base word and the preposition can be split apart by other sentence elements, with the base word staying near the front and the preposition drifting toward the end or the verb cluster.

indirect-speech.intro_tr: Indirect (reported) speech in Dutch is built with a subordinate clause: use "dat" ("that") to report statements, "of" ("whether/if") to report yes/no questions, and the original question word (wie, wat, waar, wanneer, hoe, waarom...) to report wh-questions — never combine "of" with a question word. The key structural rule is that the finite verb, which stands in 2nd position in a normal main clause, must move to the very end of the clause once "dat", "of", or a question word is added. Pronouns and possessives usually shift person (ik → hij/zij) to match who is now speaking, and tenses often (but not always) shift one step into the past when the reporting verb itself is in the past tense — if the reporting verb is present tense, no backshift is required. This topic connects directly to V2 word order, subordinate-clause verb-final order, and question formation, so mastering those first makes indirect speech much easier.

possessives-genitive.title_tr: Possessive Structures and the -s Genitive (van, Jans)
possessives-genitive.intro_tr: Dutch expresses possession in three main ways: (1) possessive pronouns like mijn (my) and zijn (his) placed before the noun, (2) the -s genitive attached directly to a person's name (Jans boek = Jan's book), and (3) the van-construction (het boek van Jan), which is the only option for common nouns and the most common choice overall. The -s genitive is a spelling minefield: whether you write plain -s, an apostrophe + s, or just an apostrophe depends entirely on the final sound of the name. This page also covers the "ons vs onze" agreement rule and the formal "van wie / wiens / wier" question forms for "whose".

adverb-formation.title_tr: Degree Adverbs and Intensifiers (heel, erg, nogal)
adverb-formation.intro_tr: Dutch has a rich set of degree adverbs (versterkende bijwoorden) like heel, erg, zeer, nogal, tamelijk, and vrij that intensify or soften adjectives and other adverbs — roughly equivalent to English "very," "quite," "rather," or "fairly." They always sit directly in front of the word they modify and never take agreement endings themselves, even though the adjective after them might. Their strength ranges from mild (een beetje) to extreme (uiterst, ontzettend), and choosing the right one is largely a matter of register: zeer and uiterst sound formal/written, while erg, heel, and colloquial prefixes like super- or kei- dominate everyday speech. A few words like erg and nogal carry extra nuance (erg can itself mean "bad"; nogal often implies "more than expected"), so this page maps out the full scale, the register differences, and the classic mistakes learners make.

pluperfect.intro_tr: The pluperfect (plusquamperfectum), equivalent to English "had done," expresses an action or state that was already completed before another point in the past. It is formed with the past tense of the auxiliary hebben or zijn (hadd- / was-were) plus the past participle, exactly like the perfect tense but with the auxiliary shifted one step further back in time. Dutch uses the pluperfect very frequently — much more consistently than English speakers might expect — especially after time conjunctions like nadat, voordat, and toen, and in unreal past conditionals with als. Choosing hebben or zijn as the auxiliary follows the exact same rules as the present perfect (perfectum).

conditional-perfect.title_tr: Conditional Perfect (zou hebben gedaan) — "would have done"
conditional-perfect.intro_tr: The conditional perfect (also called "past conditional") expresses what would have happened in a hypothetical past situation that did not actually occur — the Dutch equivalent of English "would have done". It is built from the conditional auxiliary zou/zouden plus the infinitive hebben or zijn plus a past participle, e.g. zou hebben gedaan or zou zijn gegaan. It is most often used in the result clause of an unreal past conditional sentence built with als (if), while colloquial Dutch frequently replaces the whole zou-construction with the simpler pluperfect (had gedaan) in both clauses. Word order is flexible: the three-part verb cluster can appear as "zou gedaan hebben" (red order) or "zou hebben gedaan" (green order), and in subordinate clauses the finite zou can shift to before or after the cluster.

passive-tenses.intro_tr: Dutch has two passive "voices": the action passive (handelingspassief) built with worden, and the state passive (toestandspassief) built with zijn, which describes the resulting condition rather than the event itself. Because worden and zijn are ordinary conjugating verbs, the tense of the passive sentence is shown simply by changing the tense of worden/zijn (wordt → present, werd → past, is/was → perfect tenses), while the main verb stays as a past participle at the end of the clause. A well-known quirk of Dutch is that the present perfect and past perfect passive normally drop the participle "geworden", so "is gedaan" can mean either "is done" (state) or "has been done" (action) — context tells you which. Modal verbs (moeten, kunnen, willen...) combine with worden to form passive sentences with obligation, ability, or desire, producing verb clusters at the end of the sentence.

infinitive-clusters.intro_tr: In Dutch, verbs like laten (to let / to have something done), zien (to see), horen (to hear), voelen (to feel), helpen (to help) and leren (to teach/learn) can combine directly with a bare infinitive (no 'te') to form a single verb cluster — similar to English 'I saw him leave' or 'I let her go'. This is often called an infinitive cluster or AcI (accusative + infinitive) construction, and it typically places an optional object between the conjugated verb and the infinitive. In compound tenses (perfect, pluperfect) these verbs trigger the IPP effect (Infinitivus Pro Participio): the expected past participle is replaced by the bare infinitive itself, e.g. 'Ik heb hem zien lopen' (never 'gezien lopen'). Getting the word order right — especially inside subordinate clauses — is essential for natural, idiomatic B2-level Dutch.

laten-causative.intro_tr: The verb "laten" is Dutch's all-purpose causative verb, roughly matching English "have/get something done" or "let/allow someone to do something." It combines with a bare infinitive that is pushed to the end of the clause, forming a two-verb cluster (or three-verb cluster in the perfect tense). A key trap for learners is the perfect tense: instead of the expected past participle "gelaten," Dutch uses the bare infinitive "laten" again when it is paired with another infinitive — a pattern called the IPP effect (infinitivus pro participio), shared with verbs like "zien," "horen," and the modals. "Laten" also appears in the reflexive construction "zich laten + infinitive" to express that something "can be done" (a passive-like potential meaning), and in the fixed imperative phrase "laten we..." meaning "let's...". Mastering "laten" requires attention to word order, the IPP rule, and its several distinct but related meanings.

inseparable-prefixes.intro_tr: Dutch has a small closed set of unstressed prefixes — be-, ver-, ont-, her- (and, less productively, ge-, mis-, er-) — that fuse permanently onto a verb stem and can never split off from it, unlike stressed separable prefixes (op-, aan-, mee-...) that detach in main clauses. These prefixes are always unstressed; the stress falls on the syllable that follows the prefix (be-SPREken, ver-AN-deren). Because the verb already begins with an unstressed prefix, its past participle is built WITHOUT the extra ge- (besproken, not gebesproken). Each prefix also carries its own typical shade of meaning: be- often makes a verb transitive or adds "thoroughly/about", ver- signals change, loss, or a mistaken action, ont- signals removal, escape, or the onset of a state, and her- means "again/re-". A handful of verbs such as voorkomen and doorzoeken exist in both a separable and an inseparable version with different meanings, distinguished purely by stress placement.

participle-adjectives.title_tr: Participles Used as Adjectives (de gelezen krant)
participle-adjectives.intro_tr: Dutch verbs have two participles — the present participle (tegenwoordig deelwoord, e.g. lezend "reading") and the past participle (voltooid deelwoord, e.g. gelezen "read") — and both can be used as ordinary adjectives in front of a noun, not just inside verb tenses like the perfectum or continuous forms. When used this way, the present participle usually expresses an active, ongoing action ("the man who is reading"), while the past participle expresses a passive, completed action ("the book that has been read"). Because these participles function exactly like adjectives, they follow the normal adjective inflection rule: add -e in most positions, but drop the -e before an indefinite singular het-word noun. A special complication is that many past participles of strong verbs already end in -en (gebroken, geschreven, gevonden), and adjectives ending in -en never take an extra -e, so those forms stay frozen no matter the context — very similar to material adjectives like houten (wooden).

word-order-inversion.intro_tr: Dutch main clauses follow the strict V2 (verb-second) rule: the finite (conjugated) verb must always occupy the second position in the sentence, no matter what occupies the first. When the subject itself sits in first position, the order looks like familiar SVO (Ik ga vandaag...). But whenever something else — a time or place adverb, a direct object, a subordinate clause, a negative word, or a discourse particle like 'toch' — is moved to the front for emphasis, contrast, or cohesion with the previous sentence, the subject must move to third position, right after the verb. This subject–verb swap is called 'inversie' (inversion), and it is one of the sharpest structural differences between Dutch and English, where SVO order stays fixed regardless of what is fronted. Mastering inversion means training yourself to always check position 2 for the verb, then find the subject wherever it lands afterward.

er-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Uses of Er (Partitive Er, Passive Dummy Subject)
er-advanced.intro_tr: "Er" is one of the hardest words in Dutch to master because it silently performs several different jobs depending on context. At beginner level you learn "er" mainly as "there is/are" (existential er). At B2 level two further, more subtle uses become important: (1) partitive er, which stands in for a noun that was just mentioned when you go on to specify how many/how much of it there is (similar to English "of them/of it"), and (2) er as a dummy subject in passive sentences whose real, logical subject is indefinite and pushed later in the sentence, or which have no object at all to promote to subject (the "subjectless passive"). Both uses are grammatically obligatory in many contexts — leaving "er" out, or using the wrong verb form after it, are among the most common mistakes English speakers make in intermediate Dutch. This page also shows when "er" must disappear again (when the subject is fronted or made definite).

rows: Introduces a new, indefinite subject with zijn/liggen/staan etc.
Replaces a place already mentioned (weak form of 'daar').
Combines with a preposition: er...aan/op/mee (see 'Pronominal Adverbs').
Stands in for a countable/mass noun already mentioned, used with a quantity word.
5. Dummy subject er in passives (this page)
Fills the empty subject slot when the real (logical) subject is indefinite and postponed.
footnotes_tr: Functions 1–3 are covered in more detail on separate pages ('er Usage', 'Pronominal Adverbs'); this page focuses on functions 4 and 5.

Partitive er is essentially obligatory in speech when the quantity word stands alone without repeating the noun.

Normal verb-final word order applies; er keeps its position relative to the quantity word.

Without context, 'Ik heb drie' is grammatical but does not refer back to anything — er is needed to link back to the noun.

relative-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Relative Clauses (wie, hetgeen, waar + preposition)
relative-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic relative pronouns die/dat/waar, Dutch uses several special forms for more abstract or formal relative constructions. "Wie" is used for people when there is no explicit antecedent noun (meaning "he/she who" or "whoever") and, in more formal or written style, after a preposition referring to a person. "Wat" is required instead of "dat" after indefinite pronouns (iets, niets, alles), after superlatives, and — most importantly — when the antecedent is not a single noun but an entire preceding clause. "Hetgeen" is a formal, mainly written synonym of clause-referring "wat". Finally, "waar" combines with a preposition (waarmee, waarover, waarin...) to replace "preposition + die/dat" whenever the antecedent is a thing, not a person.

discourse-particles.title_tr: Discourse Particles (toch, wel, maar, eens, even)
discourse-particles.intro_tr: Dutch discourse particles (modaal partikels) such as toch, wel, maar, eens, and even carry no dictionary meaning of their own — instead, they color a sentence with attitude: insistence, reassurance, softness, surprise, or casualness. English usually expresses these same nuances through intonation, extra words, or tag questions ("isn't it?", "after all", "just", "go ahead and"), which is why these tiny words are so hard to translate literally and so easy to overuse or underuse. They are always unstressed, sit right after the finite verb (and often after the subject or object pronoun), and Dutch speakers frequently stack two or more of them in a single clause for a compounded effect. Because they appear in almost every spoken sentence, mastering their placement and nuance is one of the clearest markers of natural, fluent Dutch. This topic focuses on recognizing what each particle adds emotionally/pragmatically and where it goes in the sentence, rather than on any new verb conjugation or word order rule.

comparative-clauses.intro_tr: Dutch has three key structures for building comparative and manner clauses: the correlative "hoe...hoe" (or the more formal "hoe...des te") meaning "the more..., the more...", the hypothetical comparison "alsof" meaning "as if/as though", and "zoals" meaning "as/like/such as" for comparing actions or introducing examples. Each has its own word-order rules: "hoe" and "zoals" clauses put the verb at the end (subordinate-clause order), while the second half of a "des te" construction uses main-clause inversion. Mastering these patterns lets you express proportional change, unreal comparisons, and illustrative examples fluently. This page also contrasts these connectors with related words like "als", "dan", and "net als" that students often confuse with them.

tables.caption_tr: hoe...hoe / hoe...des te — 'The more..., the more...' construction
rows: Hoe meer je leest, hoe meer je leert.

hoe + comparative..., des te + comparative + Verb + Subject
First clause verb-final; second clause has main-clause inversion (formal register)
Hoe meer je leest, des te meer leer je.
The more you read, the more you learn.
No verb needed in short fixed sayings
Each clause keeps its own subject, verb stays final

The warmer it is, the more people go to the beach.
Hoe minder je piekert, hoe rustiger je slaapt.

rows: Subordinate order: verb goes to the end

Verb-final; 'zou' marks the comparison as clearly unreal/hypothetical

She acted as if she wouldn't know me.
Literary/formal variant: main-clause inversion right after 'als', no 'of' needed

He acted as if he had heard nothing. (literary)
Same word order as plain 'alsof'; 'net' just adds emphasis

nominalization.title_tr: Verb Nominalization: het + Infinitive vs. -ing Nouns
nominalization.intro_tr: Dutch has two main strategies for turning a verb into a noun. The first is placing "het" before the bare infinitive (het lezen = "the reading" / "to read"), which is fully productive — almost any verb can be used this way — and always refers to the action or activity itself, always taking the neuter article "het". The second is attaching the suffix "-ing" to the verb stem (de lezing = "a lecture"), which creates a genuine, independent noun with its own gender (usually "de"), its own plural form, and very often a narrower or shifted meaning (a specific event, result, or institution rather than the bare, ongoing act). Because English "-ing" covers both functions at once (reading vs. a reading), English speakers frequently confuse the two Dutch forms — this page lays out exactly when and how to use each one.

men-formal-subjects.intro_tr: Dutch has two important "distancing" forms that beginners often confuse: the impersonal pronoun "men" (equivalent to English "one" / generic "you" / "people") and the formal second-person pronoun "u" (the polite equivalent of "you"). "Men" is used to make a general, faceless statement without naming who is doing the action — it always takes the same verb form as hij/zij (3rd person singular) and never changes form for object, possessive, or plural. "U" is not about generality but about politeness and social distance: it replaces jij/je when addressing strangers, elders, customers, or in formal writing, and it uses the same verb conjugation as jij/je (except for a few fixed exceptions like "bent/is" and "kunt/kan"). Both forms are hallmarks of formal, written, or official Dutch (ambtelijke stijl), so mastering them is essential for reading official texts, writing letters, or speaking politely to strangers.

preposition-nuance.title_tr: Fine Preposition Distinctions: op / aan / bij / tegen
preposition-nuance.intro_tr: Dutch op, aan, bij and tegen all correspond loosely to English "on/at/to/by/against", but their actual distribution is governed by fixed collocations (vaste voorzetsels) rather than by a single spatial logic, which is why English speakers constantly mix them up. Roughly: op suggests a surface, a target, or a state you're "on" (op vakantie, wachten op); aan suggests attachment, direction toward someone's attention, or ongoing work (denken aan, werken aan); bij suggests proximity, "at someone's place", or affiliation with an organisation (bij een bedrijf werken); tegen suggests physical or ideological opposition/contact (leunen tegen, protesteren tegen). Because so many verbs take a preposition purely by convention (not logic), the safest strategy at B2 is to memorise verb+preposition as a single lexical chunk rather than translating word for word. This page groups the four prepositions by core meaning, by fixed verb combinations, by confusable near-synonym pairs, and by the mistakes English speakers typically make.

negation-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic niet/geen, Dutch has a set of advanced negative adverbs that add nuance, formality, or emphasis: nauwelijks (hardly, scarcely), geenszins (by no means, not at all — formal/emphatic), and evenmin (neither, nor either — echoing a prior negative statement about a different subject). These words do not replace niet/geen in ordinary negation; instead they express degree ("barely"), strong denial, or negative agreement between clauses. Word order follows normal Dutch adverb placement rules (after the finite verb in main clauses, before the past participle/infinitive), but each item has its own typical position and register that learners must memorize individually.

triple-verb-clusters.title_tr: Triple Verb Clusters (zou hebben kunnen doen)
triple-verb-clusters.intro_tr: Dutch allows verbs to stack up to three or four deep at the end of a clause, producing chains like "zou hebben kunnen doen" (would have been able to do). These clusters combine a conditional or tense auxiliary (zou, had), a perfect auxiliary (hebben/zijn), and one or more modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen) together with a main verb, all squeezed into the clause-final "verbal end group." The key rule that makes these chains work is the Infinitivus Pro Participio (IPP): a modal verb (or laten/zien/horen/helpen) that would normally form a perfect tense with a past participle instead appears as a bare infinitive whenever it is followed by another infinitive. So "heeft gekund" never appears before another verb — it becomes "heeft ... kunnen doen." Word order inside the cluster can shift slightly between Netherlandic and Belgian Dutch, but the meaning stays the same. This is an advanced (C1) structure, so it helps to master two-verb clusters (like "had moeten doen") thoroughly before tackling triple ones.

impersonal-passive.intro_tr: The impersonal passive (onpersoonlijk passief) is a uniquely Dutch construction built from intransitive verbs (verbs with no direct object, like dansen, lachen, werken) using the dummy subject 'er' plus a form of 'worden' and the past participle. Unlike the personal passive, where an object becomes the grammatical subject, here there is no underlying object at all — the sentence simply describes that an action is happening in general, without naming who does it, much like English 'there is dancing' or 'dancing is going on'. Because 'er' is a pure placeholder with no real meaning, it can shift position or even disappear depending on what else occupies the front of the sentence. This construction is very common in notices, rules, and general statements ('Hier wordt niet gerookt' = 'No smoking here') and is a hallmark of fluent, idiomatic Dutch at higher levels.

modality-nuance.title_tr: Modality Nuances: schijnen, blijken, lijken, horen te
modality-nuance.intro_tr: Dutch has four verbs that let you fine-tune HOW certain or expected a statement is, instead of just saying "it is." Schijnen signals hearsay — you heard it somewhere but haven't verified it yourself. Blijken signals a confirmed fact or outcome, often revealed after the event. Lijken expresses a personal impression based on what you perceive right now. Horen te is not about evidence at all — it expresses a social or moral norm, i.e. what "ought" to happen. All four typically combine with "te + infinitive" (comparable to English "to be/to do"), and mastering the difference is a hallmark of near-native fluency.

subjunctive-remnants.title_tr: Fossilized Subjunctive Remnants (leve, moge, het zij zo)
subjunctive-remnants.intro_tr: Dutch lost its full subjunctive mood centuries ago, but a handful of fossilized subjunctive forms survive in fixed expressions, toasts, blessings, curses, and formal/legal or literary language. Instead of a productive grammatical system, you simply need to recognize and memorize these frozen phrases, since native speakers use them as set idioms rather than by applying a live rule. The forms typically drop the personal ending (-t/-en) that the indicative would require, leaving a bare "optative" stem such as leve, moge, or zij. Because this is a closed, memorized set, the goal at any level — including for a beginner meeting this topic early — is recognition and correct usage of the fixed phrases, not free production of new subjunctive sentences. This page collects the surviving forms, their patterns, and the most common idioms so you can spot and use them confidently.

te-infinitive-advanced.title_tr: Advanced te + Infinitive Clauses (alvorens te, zonder te)
te-infinitive-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic 'om te' construction, Dutch has a family of formal linking expressions that combine a preposition/conjunction with 'te + infinitive' to compress a subordinate idea into a compact non-finite clause: zonder te ('without doing'), alvorens te ('before doing'), in plaats van te ('instead of doing'), door te ('by doing'), and the perfect infinitive na ... te hebben/zijn ('after having done'). These constructions are common in written, formal, and literary Dutch, and they all share one strict rule: the implied subject of the te-infinitive clause must be identical to the subject of the main clause. When the subjects differ, Dutch switches to a full subordinate clause with 'dat' (zonder dat, voordat) instead. Word order inside these clauses is fixed: any object or adverb goes between the linking word and 'te + infinitive', and for separable verbs 'te' is inserted between the prefix and the stem.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: advanced te + infinitive linking expressions
footnotes_tr: 'om te' is covered in a separate topic; it is listed here only for contrast with the more formal expressions.

tables.caption_tr: zonder te + infinitive — 'without doing'
rows: The subject of 'zonder te' must equal the main clause subject
Hij ging weg zonder te betalen. (he = he)
'te' splits the prefix from the stem
zonder op te bellen (not: zonder te opbellen)
Hij vertrok zonder dat iemand het merkte.
'zonder' already carries the negative meaning; do not add 'niet'
zonder te twijfelen (not: zonder niet te twijfelen)

tables.caption_tr: alvorens te vs. voordat — expressing 'before'

Voordat hij vertrok, controleerde hij de deuren.
Alvorens hij vertrok, sprak hij nog kort met haar.
footnotes_tr: In everyday spoken Dutch, 'voordat' is far more common than 'alvorens'; 'alvorens te' typically appears in speeches, instructions, and official documents.

tables.caption_tr: The perfect infinitive: na + past participle + te hebben/zijn
rows: transitive verbs and most intransitive verbs
na het boek gelezen te hebben
verbs of motion or change of state (zijn-verbs)
na gedaan te hebben (not: na te hebben gedaan)
reflexive pronoun stays before the participle

'alvorens te' never combines with 'dat'; choose one pattern

examples.target: Na het artikel gelezen te hebben, begreep ze alles.

examples.note_tr: Perfect infinitive: participle + te hebben, placed after 'na'.

examples.target: In plaats van te klagen, moet je actie ondernemen.
examples.translation_tr: Instead of complaining, you should take action.
examples.note_tr: in plaats van te + infinitive = 'instead of doing'.

examples.target: Door hard te werken, slaagde hij voor zijn examen.
examples.translation_tr: By working hard, he passed his exam.
examples.note_tr: door te + infinitive expresses the means/method ('by doing').

examples.target: Alvorens te beginnen, wil ik iedereen bedanken.
examples.translation_tr: Before beginning, I would like to thank everyone.
examples.note_tr: Typical opening line in formal speeches; note the comma after the te-clause.

examples.target: Ze verliet het huis zonder iets te zeggen.

examples.note_tr: The object (iets) stands before 'te + infinitive', not after it.
