examples.note_tr: Irregular participle 'gegeten' still follows the pattern: participle + te hebben.

fronting-topicalization.intro_tr: Dutch is a strict V2 (verb-second) language: the finite verb must be the second element of a main clause, but the slot before it — the "front field" — can be filled by almost any single constituent, not only the subject. Speakers and writers exploit this freedom to organize information into topic (what the sentence is about, usually old/given information) and comment (the new information said about it), and to signal contrast, emphasis, or smooth continuity with the previous sentence. Whenever a non-subject element is fronted, the subject is pushed to the position right after the finite verb (subject-verb inversion) — the verb itself never moves. Mastering these patterns, and distinguishing true fronting from the superficially similar left-dislocation construction, is essential for producing cohesive, natural-sounding advanced Dutch, especially in writing.

tables.caption_tr: Types of constituents that can be fronted (neutral order vs. fronted order)
rows: Ik heb haar het boek gegeven.
Haar heb ik het boek gegeven.
Hij loste het probleem snel op.
Snel loste hij het probleem op.
Ik weet geen antwoord op die vraag.
Op die vraag weet ik geen antwoord.
To that question I don't know an answer.
Never have I seen such a thing.
Ik weet niet zeker dat hij komt.
Dat hij komt, weet ik niet zeker.
That he's coming, I'm not sure of.
Ik heb het boek niet gelezen.
Gelezen heb ik het boek niet.
Read, I haven't (the book) — but maybe I've seen it.

tables.caption_tr: Mechanics: subject-verb inversion after fronting
rows: The subject already occupies position 1, so the order stays Subject–Verb–Object.
The finite verb keeps position 2; the subject is pushed to the slot right after the verb.
Only ONE constituent per front field
A multi-word phrase can be fronted only if it forms a single syntactic unit; you cannot front two separate constituents at once.
Vorige week zaterdag ben ik naar Parijs geweest. (one time phrase, correct) / *Vorige week naar Parijs ben ik geweest. (two separate constituents, incorrect)
The finite verb never moves from position 2
Fronting changes what precedes the verb, never the verb's own position.
Gisteren heb ik hem gezien. (heb stays in position 2)

tables.caption_tr: Discourse functions: why speakers front elements
rows: Front an element already established in the discourse to keep the topic in focus and avoid a monotonous subject-first style.
Jan kocht een boek. Het boek heeft hij meteen gelezen.
Smooth cohesion between sentences; 'het boek' stays the shared thread.
Front an element to contrast it explicitly with something mentioned before or after.
Koffie drink ik niet, maar thee wel.
Highlights the opposition between coffee and tea.
Fronting adverbs like nooit, zelden, nauwelijks for rhetorical or literary emphasis.
Dramatic, formal, emphatic tone (similar to English 'Never have I...').
Front time or place adverbials to establish the frame before narrating the event.
Typical of narrative and news-style writing.
In answers, front the element that was questioned.
Wie zag je? — Jan zag ik.
The fronted element directly answers the wh-question.

tables.caption_tr: Topicalization (fronting) vs. left-dislocation — do not confuse them
rows: Absent — the fronted phrase IS the argument
Obligatory — a pronoun (die, dat, hij, ze...) fills the grammatical slot
No comma between fronted element and finite verb
Comma (or intonation break) after the dislocated phrase
Die film heb ik al gezien.
Die film, die heb ik al gezien.
Word order after the fronted element
Full clause with normal order follows, headed by the resumptive pronoun
Neutral to formal; used in all styles including writing
More colloquial/spoken, strongly emphatic or list-like

tables.caption_tr: Special cases and restrictions
rows: Fronted subordinate clause needs a comma
When an entire dat-, of-, or als-clause is fronted, it is separated from the main clause by a comma before the finite verb.
Als het regent, blijf ik thuis. / Dat hij gelijk heeft, betwijfel ik.
The bare particle of a separable verb can be fronted alone, still triggering inversion; this is marked/literary.
Op staat hij meteen. (= Hij staat meteen op.)
The non-finite verb form can be fronted while the finite auxiliary stays in position 2, contrasting the action itself.
Gedaan heb ik het wel, maar niet goed.
Weak, unstressed er normally appears in position 1 only as a default expletive, not as a deliberately fronted focus element.
Er staat een man voor de deur. (default existential order, not contrastive fronting)
Fronting is blocked for parts of fixed idioms
You cannot extract and front just one word out of a fixed collocation or idiomatic verb-object pair without breaking the idiom's meaning.
*Been heeft hij het (from 'het been breken' meaning something idiomatic) — generally avoided if it destroys the fixed reading.

examples.target: De kat zie ik niet.
examples.translation_tr: The cat, I don't see (it). / I don't see the cat.
examples.note_tr: The direct object 'de kat' is fronted for contrast or topic continuity; the finite verb 'zie' stays in position 2 and the subject 'ik' follows it (inversion).

examples.target: Gisteren heb ik hem op straat gezien.
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday I saw him on the street.
examples.note_tr: A time adverbial is fronted to set the scene; this is extremely common in narrative and news style.

examples.target: Nooit heb ik zoiets grappigs gehoord.
examples.translation_tr: Never have I heard something so funny.
examples.note_tr: Fronting a negative adverb like 'nooit' creates dramatic, formal emphasis, similar to inversion after 'never' in English.

examples.target: Dat hij de waarheid spreekt, betwijfel ik ten zeerste.
examples.translation_tr: That he is telling the truth, I doubt very much.
examples.note_tr: A whole 'dat'-clause functions as one constituent and is fronted; note the comma before the main clause's finite verb.

examples.target: Moe was ze niet, maar wel een beetje verdrietig.
examples.translation_tr: Tired she was not, but she was a little sad.
examples.note_tr: The predicate adjective 'moe' is fronted to set up a contrast with what follows.

examples.target: Koffie drink ik niet meer, maar thee drink ik graag.
examples.translation_tr: I no longer drink coffee, but I do like tea.
examples.note_tr: Classic contrastive topicalization: each object is fronted in its own clause to highlight the opposition between the two drinks.

examples.target: Op die vraag heb ik helaas geen antwoord.
examples.translation_tr: To that question, I unfortunately have no answer.
examples.note_tr: A prepositional phrase is fronted as a single constituent; the subject 'ik' follows the finite verb 'heb'.

examples.target: Die film, die heb ik al drie keer gezien.
examples.translation_tr: That movie, I've already seen it three times.
examples.note_tr: This is left-dislocation, not simple fronting: the topic 'die film' sits outside the clause (comma) and a resumptive pronoun 'die' fills the object slot inside the clause.

cleft-sentences.intro_tr: Cleft sentences (Dutch: "gespleten zinnen") split an ordinary sentence into two parts in order to put special emphasis on one element, using the fixed frame "Het is/zijn ... die/dat ...", very similar to English "It is ... that/who ...". The element you want to highlight — subject, object, or even an adverbial phrase — is placed directly after "het is/zijn", while the rest of the sentence becomes a relative-clause-like tail introduced by "die" or "dat", with the finite verb pushed to the end. The choice between "die" and "dat" follows the same de-word/het-word/plural logic used in ordinary relative clauses, and "is" versus "zijn" simply agrees with whether the highlighted element is singular or plural. Cleft sentences are very common in formal writing, in contrastive statements ("not X but Y"), and in direct answers to questions, and they can also be used to front adverbial phrases of time, place, or reason (always with "dat").

tables.caption_tr: Basic cleft sentence formula
rows: Het is de leraar die het uitlegt. (It is the teacher who explains it.)
Het is het boek dat op tafel ligt. (It is the book that is on the table.)
Het zijn de studenten die slagen. (It is the students who pass.)
Object referring to a person / de-word
Het is Marie die ik gisteren zag. (It is Marie whom I saw yesterday.)
Het is dit huis dat wij willen kopen. (It is this house that we want to buy.)

tables.caption_tr: Choosing die vs. dat after the highlighted element
rows: Het is de auto die kapot is. (It is the car that is broken.)
Het is het huis dat te koop staat. (It is the house that is for sale.)
Het zijn de kinderen die spelen. (It is the children who are playing.)
Het is hij die het zei. (It is he who said it.)
Het is daarom dat ik het doe. (That is why I do it.)

tables.caption_tr: Copula agreement (is / zijn) across tenses
Clefting non-noun elements (adverbials and clauses)
rows: Het is Jan die het weet. (It is Jan who knows it.)
Het is in 1990 dat hij geboren werd. (It was in 1990 that he was born.)
Het is hier dat het gebeurde. (It is here that it happened.)
Het is om die reden dat ik niet kom. (It is for that reason that I am not coming.)
Het is omdat hij ziek was dat hij niet kwam. (It is because he was ill that he did not come.)

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with cleft sentences
rows: Het is de studenten die slagen.
Het zijn de studenten die slagen.
Use 'zijn' instead of 'is' when the highlighted noun is plural.
Het is het boek die ik lees.
Het is het boek dat ik lees.
'boek' is a het-word, so the connector must be 'dat', not 'die'.
Het was de kinderen die speelden.
Het waren de kinderen die speelden.
Past tense with a plural element requires 'waren', not 'was'.
Het is Jan wie het zei.
Het is Jan die het zei.
'wie' is not used here; use 'die' for people in cleft/relative constructions.
Het is daar die het gebeurde.
Het is daar dat het gebeurde.
Adverbial phrases (time/place/reason) are always followed by 'dat', never 'die'.

examples.target: Het is het boek dat ik gisteren gekocht heb.
examples.translation_tr: It is the book that I bought yesterday. ('boek' is a het-word, so 'dat' is used)

examples.target: Het zijn de kinderen die buiten spelen.
examples.translation_tr: It is the children who are playing outside. (plural emphasized element → 'zijn' and 'die')

examples.target: Het was mijn moeder die belde.
examples.translation_tr: It was my mother who called. (past tense, singular → 'was ... die')

examples.target: Het waren de buren die klaagden.
examples.translation_tr: It was the neighbors who complained. (past tense, plural → 'waren ... die')

examples.target: Het is niet Peter maar Marie die gelijk heeft.
examples.translation_tr: It is not Peter but Marie who is right. (contrastive cleft)

examples.target: Is het Anna die morgen komt?
examples.translation_tr: Is it Anna who is coming tomorrow? (cleft in a yes/no question)

examples.target: Het is om die reden dat ik niet kom.
examples.translation_tr: It is for that reason that I am not coming. (adverbial phrase highlighted, always followed by 'dat')

correlative-conjunctions.intro_tr: Correlative conjunctions are conjunction pairs that link two parallel elements (words, phrases, or clauses) and express relationships such as "both...and", "neither...nor", or "either...or". In Dutch the most important pairs are zowel...als (both...and), noch...noch (neither...nor), hetzij...hetzij / of...of (either...or), en...en (both...and, more emphatic/older style), and niet alleen...maar (ook) (not only...but also). These pairs are a hallmark of formal, written, and argumentative Dutch (essays, reports, legal and academic texts) and are largely avoided in casual speech, where simpler en, of, or maar are preferred. A key grammatical trap is noch...noch, which is inherently negative and therefore cannot be combined with niet or geen, and it can trigger special verb agreement and word-order effects when placed at the start of a sentence. Mastering these pairs, their register, and their word-order behavior (especially inversion when the pair opens the sentence) is essential for producing polished C1-level Dutch.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of Dutch correlative conjunction pairs
rows: neutral to formal, common in writing and speech
joining two nouns, adjectives, phrases, or clauses that both apply
stressing that two things are simultaneously true
negating two alternatives together; replaces niet...en niet
presenting two (or more) mutually exclusive options
neutral, very common in speech and writing
adding emphasis to a second element beyond the first
splitting a situation into two partial causes/aspects

tables.caption_tr: Word order with correlative conjunctions
rows: normal declarative order; the pair simply connects the two elements, no inversion
Zowel de leraar als de leerlingen waren tevreden. (Both the teacher and the students were satisfied.)
Mid-sentence, linking two clauses (each with its own verb)
each clause keeps its own normal V2 order
Hij werkt zowel hard als hij studeert veel. (informal use — more natural with 'en')
triggers inversion in the following main clause: subject follows the finite verb
Noch Jan noch Piet heeft de sleutel. (Neither Jan nor Piet has the key.)
each hetzij-clause can keep normal order; no inversion required, but formal texts often invert for emphasis
Hetzij hij komt, hetzij hij belt af. (Either he comes, or he cancels.)
niet alleen at the start of a clause
triggers inversion: niet alleen + verb + subject...
Niet alleen won hij de wedstrijd, maar hij verbrak ook het record. (Not only did he win the match, but he also broke the record.)

tables.caption_tr: Special behavior of noch...noch (negative pair)
rows: noch already carries negation, so adding niet or geen creates a double negative error
Correct: Hij heeft noch tijd noch geld. / Incorrect: Hij heeft niet noch tijd noch geld.
when noch...noch joins two singular subjects, the verb is often singular in careful writing, though plural is also heard
Noch de directeur noch de secretaris is/zijn aanwezig. (Neither the director nor the secretary is/are present.)
noch...noch is the elegant written alternative to stringing together niet with en
Formal: Hij eet noch vlees noch vis. / Informal: Hij eet geen vlees en geen vis.
Can join more than two elements
noch can be repeated for three or more negated items
Noch geld, noch macht, noch roem interesseert hem. (Neither money, nor power, nor fame interests him.)

tables.caption_tr: Correlative pairs vs. simple conjunctions: register comparison
rows: niet alleen...maar ook (used in both registers, but 'ook' is often dropped informally)

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with correlative conjunctions
rows: Hij spreekt zowel Engels en Nederlands.
zowel must be paired with als, not en
Hij spreekt zowel Engels als Nederlands.
Hij heeft niet noch geld noch tijd.
noch already negates; adding niet is a double negative
Hij heeft noch geld noch tijd.
Zowel hij als zij zijn niet gekomen.
mixing zowel...als (positive pairing) with a negated verb can be ambiguous; prefer noch...noch for a fully negative meaning
Noch hij noch zij is gekomen.
the two halves of a correlative pair must match; hetzij must be closed with hetzij, not of

sounds overly formal/legalistic in everyday speech
Use of...of instead in spoken Dutch.

examples.translation_tr: Both my father and my mother are coming to the party.

examples.target: Je kunt hetzij per e-mail hetzij per telefoon reageren.

formal-prepositional-phrases.title_tr: Formal Prepositional Phrases (ten aanzien van, met betrekking tot)
formal-prepositional-phrases.intro_tr: Formal prepositional phrases are multi-word units (usually preposition + noun + preposition) that Dutch uses instead of a simple preposition to sound official, precise, or bureaucratic. They are everywhere in legal texts, government letters, academic writing, news reports, and business correspondence, but almost never in everyday speech, where a single preposition or a subordinate clause does the same job. Many of them preserve a fossilized dative/genitive noun (e.g. 'ten' before a masculine/feminine noun, 'ten' + neuter noun) left over from older Dutch case endings, so their internal grammar cannot be freely changed — they must be learned as fixed chunks. Recognizing this register is a key C1 skill: you need to understand these phrases when reading official Dutch, and know when it is appropriate (and when it is stylistically odd) to use them yourself.

ten gevolge van / als gevolg van
within the framework of / as part of
on the basis of / on the grounds of

text-connectors.intro_tr: Text connectors (verbindingswoorden) are sentence-initial or mid-clause adverbs that show how one sentence logically relates to the previous one: addition, contrast, cause/result, or conclusion. Unlike coordinating conjunctions (en, maar, want) that sit between two clauses, connectors like bovendien, daarentegen, and desondanks typically open a new main clause and, when placed first, trigger V2 subject-verb inversion. Choosing the right connector is a hallmark of C1 writing: it signals register (formal vs. casual) and precise logical nuance (a strong contrast vs. a mild concession, a listed addition vs. a summary). This page groups connectors by function, shows the word-order rules they obey, and flags classic confusions such as tenslotte vs. ten slotte or desondanks vs. ondanks dat.

tables.caption_tr: Additive Connectors (adding further supporting information)
rows: Adds a stronger/decisive extra point; in first position it forces inversion.
Very common in speech and writing; literally 'next to that'.
Typical of official, business, or legal texts.
Also literally means 'further'; frequent in spoken Dutch.
Rare in speech; found in reports and legal documents.

tables.caption_tr: Contrastive & Concessive Connectors
rows: on the other hand, in contrast
Sets up a direct contrast between two parallel statements, often paired with 'terwijl' in the first clause.
Often placed after the subject/first constituent rather than clause-initial, giving a softer contrast.
Very flexible position, can appear mid-clause; softer/weaker than desondanks.
Refers back to a previously mentioned obstacle or fact.
More literary than toch or desondanks; common in essays.

tables.caption_tr: Causal & Consequential Connectors
rows: because of that, as a result
Refers to a concrete cause producing a concrete effect.
Extremely common; can be clause-initial or mid-clause.
Explains a reason that was already given.
Rare in everyday speech; typical of legal texts.
Typical of academic or argumentative writing.
Emphasizes the manner or process leading to the result.

tables.caption_tr: Sequencing & Concluding Connectors
rows: Marks the next step in a sequence of events.
Marks the last of several steps or points.
Introduces a justifying afterthought, NOT a sequence step; easily confused with 'ten slotte'.
Summative; often closes a text or paragraph.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and False Friends
rows: 'ondanks' is a preposition and needs a noun object; it cannot stand alone as a connector
Desondanks kwam hij niet. / Ondanks dat kwam hij niet.
Use 'desondanks' (connector) or 'ondanks dat' (subordinator) to link two full clauses.
Using 'tenslotte' for the last item in a list
Ten slotte hebben we het dessert geserveerd.
Use the two-word form 'ten slotte' for 'lastly/finally' in a sequence of steps.
Hij is ziek, daarentegen hij werkt door.

Hij is ziek; hij werkt daarentegen door.

forgetting V2 inversion after a fronted connector
Any adverbial connector placed in position 1 forces subject–verb inversion.

examples.note_tr: Desondanks refers back to the fact just mentioned (being ill).

examples.translation_tr: The traffic was jammed, so as a result we arrived late.
examples.note_tr: Daardoor links a concrete cause to its concrete effect.

examples.target: Ze is moe; toch blijft ze doorwerken.
examples.translation_tr: She is tired; still, she keeps on working.
examples.note_tr: Toch is more informal/flexible than desondanks and niettemin.

examples.target: Ten slotte wil ik de organisatoren bedanken.
examples.translation_tr: Finally, I would like to thank the organizers.
examples.note_tr: Two-word 'ten slotte' marks the last item in a sequence.

examples.translation_tr: He doesn't like traveling; after all, he hasn't been outside the Netherlands for sixty years.
examples.note_tr: One-word 'tenslotte' introduces a justifying afterthought, not a sequence step.

examples.translation_tr: In short, the project was a success.
examples.note_tr: Kortom summarizes everything stated before it.

word-formation.intro_tr: Dutch builds a huge share of its vocabulary through derivational suffixes rather than borrowing new words. The four suffixes -heid, -baar, -lijk and -achtig let you turn adjectives, nouns and verb stems into new adjectives or abstract nouns, which is essential for reading academic and formal Dutch fluently. -heid creates de-word abstract nouns from adjectives (vrij → vrijheid), -baar creates "-able" adjectives from verb stems (lezen → leesbaar), -lijk creates "-ly/-like/-able" adjectives from nouns or verbs (vriend → vriendelijk), and -achtig creates "-ish/resembling" adjectives from nouns or adjectives (groen → groenachtig). These suffixes can even be chained (mogen → mogelijk → mogelijkheid), and each has its own spelling quirks and irregular plurals worth memorizing at an advanced level.

compound-nouns.intro_tr: Dutch builds long compound nouns by joining two or more words into a single written unit, where English would often use separate words or a hyphen (e.g., boekenkast = "bookcase", regeringsleider = "head of government"). The final element — the head — always determines the whole compound's gender (de/het) and how it forms its plural; only the head can be pluralized. Between the parts, Dutch may insert a linking sound (tussenklank) — the linking -s- or the linking -en- — or use no linking sound at all, depending mainly on the ending and plural form of the first word. Reliable patterns exist (suffixes like -ing, -heid, -teit, -schap, -dom favor -s-; nouns whose plural ends in -en often favor -en-), but many everyday compounds are irregular and simply have to be memorized. The tables below group the dependable rules together with the key exceptions and spelling/hyphenation quirks you will meet most often.

tables.caption_tr: Core Rules for Building Dutch Compound Nouns
rows: No space and, usually, no hyphen between the parts
The final noun carries the core meaning of the whole compound

de/het of the compound = de/het of the last noun
Only the final element takes a plural ending
The first part carries the primary stress, the rest is unstressed
Part 1 narrows or describes part 2 (opposite of many English patterns)
fietsband = tire OF a bike (band + fiets)

rows: Noun already ending in a vowel

examples.note_tr: auto-ongeluk needs a hyphen to avoid an awkward vowel collision; ziekenhuis uses -en- (ziek → zieken).

punctuation-style.intro_tr: Dutch spelling has a handful of small but high-frequency rules that trip up even advanced learners: the "tussen-n" (linking -n-) that appears inside many compound nouns, the apostrophe used to form plurals and possessives of vowel-ending words, the trema (diaeresis) that separates vowels that would otherwise merge into one sound, and the hyphen inserted between compound parts when two identical vowels would collide. None of these are optional stylistic choices — they are governed by fixed, checkable rules (mostly based on how the first word pluralizes) that the official Dutch spelling authority (Taalunie) codifies. This page collects the core rules, exceptions, and the apostrophe's several unrelated jobs (plural, possessive, omitted letters) in one place so you stop guessing.

tables.caption_tr: The tussen-n (linking -n-) rule in compound nouns

Write -en- if the first noun's plural ends in -en, even if the compound as a whole is singular in meaning
kippenhok (a coop for one or many chickens)

archaic-case-remnants.title_tr: Fixed Expressions and Fossilized Case Remnants (der, des, te allen tijde)
archaic-case-remnants.intro_tr: Modern Dutch lost its case system centuries ago, but a small, closed set of fossilized case endings and articles survives in fixed expressions, formal titles, church/legal language, and everyday time phrases. Forms like der, des, den, ten and ter are frozen remnants of the old genitive and dative cases: they are NOT productive — you cannot invent new phrases with them, you can only memorize the existing ones as vocabulary chunks. Recognizing them helps you read older texts, legal/religious language, and formal writing, and also explains oddities like 's ochtends or ten slotte that beginners often mislearn as irregular exceptions. This page collects the whole closed inventory so you never need to guess.

literary-tenses.title_tr: Literary Narrative Tenses and the Historical Present
literary-tenses.intro_tr: Dutch literary and narrative prose does not simply follow the ordinary rules of tense that govern spoken or everyday written Dutch: it uses the historisch presens (historical present) to inject immediacy into past events, alternates freely between imperfectum and plusquamperfectum to layer main events and background/flashback, and employs vrije indirecte rede (free indirect speech) to blend the narrator's voice with a character's inner thoughts without formal markers like 'dat' or quotation marks. This register also preserves archaic or elevated conjugated forms (such as 'zeide' or the relic subjunctive 'ware') that have disappeared from spoken Dutch but survive in literary, journalistic, or ceremonial writing. Mastering these devices is essential for reading Dutch literature, older texts, and stylistically ambitious journalism, and for producing sophisticated, C2-level written narration yourself.

Highlights a completed result still relevant to the narrative moment; also used in frame narration where a present-tense narrator reports on past events

complex-passive-transforms.intro_tr: Dutch has three distinct passive constructions that are often collapsed into one 'passive voice' in English: the worden-passive (a process/action happening to the direct object), the zijn-passive (the resulting state after that action), and the krijgen-passive (used when the recipient — the indirect object of a ditransitive verb — becomes the subject). The krijgen-passive is the closest Dutch equivalent of English constructions like 'I was given a book' or 'She got told off', and it cannot be formed with worden. A key advanced trap is that in perfect and pluperfect tenses the extra past participle of the main verb (e.g. gegeven) is normally dropped, because krijgen itself already carries the meaning 'to receive'. Combining krijgen-passives with modal verbs, future tense, and embedded clauses produces the complex passive transformations covered here.

rows: an action/process happening to the direct object
De leraar geeft de leerling een boek. (The teacher gives the student a book.)
Het boek wordt aan de leerling gegeven. (The book is given to the student.)
the resulting state after the action is complete
Het boek is (al) gegeven. (The book has (already) been given.)
De leraar geeft de leerling een boek.
De leerling krijgt een boek gegeven. (The student is given a book.)
footnotes_tr: Only ditransitive verbs (verbs with both a direct and an indirect object) can form a krijgen-passive.
worden = process ('is being done'); zijn = state ('has been done, is now finished').

tables.caption_tr: Full tense conjugation of the krijgen-passive (example: iemand geeft mij een cadeau — someone gives me a present)
rows: I have been given / received a present.
I had been given / received a present.
I will be given a present.
I would be given a present.
footnotes_tr: In the perfect and pluperfect, the second past participle (gegeven) is normally dropped — 'Ik heb een cadeau gegeven gekregen' is redundant and sounds unnatural, though it does occur informally for extra clarity.
In the future and conditional, the past participle is almost always omitted entirely.

tables.caption_tr: Transforming an active sentence into worden- vs. krijgen-passive
rows: De directeur beloofde de werknemer een bonus.
The director promised the employee a bonus.
Een bonus werd (door de directeur) aan de werknemer beloofd.
A bonus was promised to the employee (by the director).
De werknemer kreeg een bonus beloofd (door de directeur).
The employee was promised a bonus (by the director).
footnotes_tr: The agent (door + noun) is optional and often omitted in both passive types, but is more natural to keep with worden than with krijgen.

tables.caption_tr: Modal verbs combined with passive constructions
rows: He is allowed to receive a present.
modal + krijgen + participle (future obligation on recipient)
Zij zal een waarschuwing krijgen gestuurd.
She will be sent a warning.
laten + infinitive (causative, not a true passive)
He has the house painted (by someone else).
footnotes_tr: With krijgen, adding a modal often shifts the meaning from pure passive to permission or future certainty rather than obligation on the subject itself.
laten is included here only for contrast: it is causative, and the subject is the initiator, not the recipient.

tables.caption_tr: Common ditransitive verbs that allow a krijgen-passive
rows: De baas belooft de werknemers een verhoging.
De werknemers krijgen een verhoging beloofd.
De school biedt de student een beurs aan.
De student krijgt een beurs aangeboden.
De gids toont de toeristen het schilderij.
De toeristen krijgen het schilderij getoond.
De rechter wijst het kind aan de moeder toe.
Het kind krijgt aan de moeder toegewezen.
De bank weigert hem een lening.

tables.caption_tr: Common errors with the krijgen-passive
rows: Calques English 'I am given'; worden cannot promote an indirect object to subject.
Het boek krijgt gegeven aan de leerling.
krijgen-passive needs a recipient as subject, not the item itself.
Het boek wordt aan de leerling gegeven.
Ik heb een cadeau gegeven gekregen.
Redundant double participle in the perfect tense; sounds unnatural in written Dutch.
zien is monotransitive (no indirect object), so it cannot form a krijgen-passive.
helpen normally takes only a direct object in standard Dutch, so worden is preferred.
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: krijgen-passive is possible only when the verb has a clear indirect object (someone 'receives' something) in the active sentence.

examples.target: De leerling krijgt een compliment gegeven door de leraar.
examples.translation_tr: The student is given a compliment by the teacher.
examples.note_tr: krijgen-passive: the indirect object (de leerling) becomes the subject.

examples.target: Ik heb gisteren een uitnodiging gekregen.
examples.translation_tr: I received/was given an invitation yesterday.
examples.note_tr: Perfect tense: the extra participle (gegeven) is dropped — only 'gekregen' is used.

examples.target: Het pakket wordt morgen bezorgd.
examples.translation_tr: The package will be delivered tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: Ordinary worden-passive for comparison: the direct object (het pakket) is the subject.

examples.target: Zij kreeg de opdracht toegewezen.
examples.translation_tr: She was assigned the task.
examples.note_tr: Past tense krijgen-passive with the ditransitive verb 'toewijzen'.

examples.target: Het probleem moet zo snel mogelijk opgelost worden.
examples.translation_tr: The problem must be solved as soon as possible.
examples.note_tr: Modal + passive infinitive (moeten + worden + participle) — no krijgen equivalent here since there is no indirect object.

examples.target: Hij zal waarschijnlijk een boete krijgen opgelegd.
examples.translation_tr: He will probably be given a fine.
examples.note_tr: Future tense krijgen-passive; 'opgelegd' can be dropped in casual speech: 'Hij zal een boete krijgen.'

examples.target: De brief was al verstuurd toen ze hem kreeg getoond.
examples.translation_tr: The letter had already been sent when she was shown it.
examples.note_tr: Combines a zijn-passive (state: was al verstuurd) with a krijgen-passive (kreeg getoond) in one sentence.

examples.target: Nadat ze de prijs had gekregen, bedankte ze iedereen.
examples.translation_tr: After she had received/been given the prize, she thanked everyone.
examples.note_tr: Pluperfect krijgen-passive: 'had gekregen' — again no extra participle needed.

ellipsis-gapping.intro_tr: Ellipsis and gapping are advanced syntactic phenomena in which recoverable material (typically the finite verb, a verb cluster, a noun, or an entire clause) is left unpronounced because it can be reconstructed from a parallel clause or from the discourse context. Dutch relies heavily on such omissions in coordinated sentences (en, maar), comparative clauses (dan, als), correlative structures (hoe...hoe), and short answers, where repeating the verb or noun would sound clumsy or redundant. A key distinction is made between "gapping" (deleting only the verb, leaving two or more contrastive remnants on either side), "stripping" (reducing an entire clause to a single remnant plus a polarity/additive particle like wel, niet, ook), and "VP-ellipsis" (dropping an infinitive or verb cluster after a modal/auxiliary). Because Dutch is a strict V2 language in main clauses, gapped conjuncts behave differently from normal clauses: once the finite verb is gapped, the remaining V2 constraint no longer applies to that conjunct, which produces word-order patterns that look "SOV-like" to learners. Mastering these patterns is essential for producing natural, non-repetitive written and spoken Dutch at a near-native level.

tables.caption_tr: Main Types of Ellipsis in Dutch
rows: the finite verb (sometimes with other shared material)
Jan eet appels en Marie peren.
Jan eet appels en Marie eet peren.
an entire clause, leaving one remnant + a particle
Jan komt morgen, en Piet ook.
Jan komt morgen, en Piet komt morgen ook.
the infinitive(s) governed by a modal or auxiliary
Ik kan het niet, maar hij wel.
Ik kan het niet, maar hij kan het wel.
the repeated verb (and sometimes subject) after dan/als
Hij is groter dan ik ben.
the head noun after a numeral or adjective
Ik heb twee auto's, hij drie.
Ik heb twee auto's, hij heeft drie auto's.
the whole clause in a short answer
a shared final constituent, pronounced only once
Jan wast en Marie droogt de auto.
Jan wast de auto en Marie droogt de auto.
footnotes_tr: All types require that the omitted material be fully recoverable from the surrounding sentence or discourse; ambiguous ellipsis is avoided in careful writing.

tables.caption_tr: Structural Rules for Gapping in Coordination
rows: Only the finite verb (or full verb cluster) is gapped
Objects, subjects and adverbials cannot be gapped alone while leaving the verb behind.
Jan gaf Marie een boek en Piet Anna een cd. (verb 'gaf' gapped, four remnants remain)
The surviving constituents are the ones being compared/contrasted between the two conjuncts.
Jan werkt in Utrecht en Piet in Rotterdam.
V2 no longer applies in the gapped conjunct
Because the finite verb is absent, the remnants line up in a flat Subject–Object–Adverbial order instead of verb-second order.
Jan eet appels en Marie morgen peren. (not: *Jan eet appels en morgen Marie peren.)
It is much less natural or impossible with maar/of, which normally trigger stripping instead.
Jan eet appels en Marie peren. (natural) vs. ?Jan eet appels maar Marie peren. (odd)
The verb must be semantically/formally recoverable
If the two conjuncts would need different tense or modality on the missing verb, gapping is blocked.
*Jan at appels en Marie eet peren. → must repeat the verb: Jan at appels en Marie at peren.

tables.caption_tr: Stripping and Answer Particles
rows: Jan komt morgen, en Piet ook.
Jan komt niet, en Piet ook niet.
affirmative contrast after a negated clause
Ik kan het niet, maar hij wel.
negative contrast after an affirmative clause
Hij wil wel, maar ik niet.
Niet Jan komt, alleen Piet komt.
footnotes_tr: Stripping always keeps at least one remnant (usually the subject) plus a particle; the particle alone without any remnant is not acceptable in standard Dutch.

tables.caption_tr: Comparative and Correlative Ellipsis
rows: verb (and subject, if identical) of the dan-clause may be dropped
Zij werkt harder dan hij werkt.
verb of the als-clause is typically dropped
Hij is even groot als zij.
Hij is even groot als zij groot is.
the shared predicate (often 'het is') is obligatorily gapped in fixed expressions
Hoe meer het is, hoe beter het is.
Hij is zo sterk als een beer.
Hij is zo sterk als een beer sterk is.
footnotes_tr: In formal writing, retaining the verb in dan/als-clauses (dan hij werkt) is also correct and sometimes preferred for clarity; ellipsis is the more common, less formal choice.

tables.caption_tr: Nominal Ellipsis After Numerals and Adjectives
rows: Ik heb twee katten, zij drie.
Ik heb twee katten, zij heeft drie katten.
The verb 'heeft' is also gapped here alongside the noun.
De grote auto en de kleine staan buiten.
De grote auto en de kleine auto staan buiten.
The adjective keeps its inflectional -e even though the noun is dropped.
Ik neem de rode, niet die blauwe.
Using a demonstrative is a common alternative strategy to true noun ellipsis.
Dit boek is goed, dat andere niet.
Dit boek is goed, dat andere boek niet.
Ellipsis after 'ander(e)' is very frequent in everyday speech.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Ellipsis and Gapping
rows: *Jan eet appels en morgen Marie peren.
An adverbial cannot be fronted before the subject in a gapped conjunct because there is no verb left to license V2 word order there.
Jan eet appels en Marie morgen peren.
*Jan at appels en Marie eet peren.
Gapping requires the two verbs to match in tense/mood; a mismatched tense blocks recovery of the gapped verb.
Jan at appels en Marie at peren. (or repeat the verb explicitly)
Stripping needs an overt remnant (usually the subject) in addition to the particle; the particle alone is not a valid short answer.
Ga je mee? — Ja, ik wel.
Once the noun is elided in one conjunct for contrast, it should normally be elided consistently, or spelled out in both — mixing is stylistically inconsistent.
Ik heb twee auto's, hij drie. / Ik heb twee auto's, hij heeft drie auto's.
The additive particle 'ook' attaches after the remnant subject, not before it, in stripped clauses.

examples.target: Jan eet appels en Marie peren.
examples.translation_tr: Jan eats apples and Mary [eats] pears. — the verb 'eet' is gapped (omitted) in the second clause because it is recoverable from the first.
examples.note_tr: Gapping: only the two contrasted remnants 'Marie' and 'peren' survive.

examples.target: Ik kan het niet, maar hij wel.
examples.translation_tr: I can't do it, but he can. — 'wel' stands in for the whole elided clause 'hij kan het wel'.
examples.note_tr: Stripping with the polarity particle 'wel' after a modal verb.

examples.target: Zij werkt harder dan hij.
examples.translation_tr: She works harder than he [does]. — the repeated verb 'werkt' is dropped after 'dan'.
examples.note_tr: Comparative ellipsis.

examples.target: Ga je mee? — Ja, ik wel.
examples.translation_tr: "Are you coming along?" — "Yes, I am." (literally: yes, I indeed)
examples.note_tr: Answer ellipsis / stripping reduces the whole reply to subject + particle.

examples.target: Jan komt morgen, en Piet ook.
examples.translation_tr: Jan is coming tomorrow, and so is Piet. — the full clause 'Piet komt morgen ook' is stripped down to 'Piet ook'.
examples.note_tr: Additive stripping with 'ook'.

examples.target: Ik heb twee katten, zij drie.
examples.translation_tr: I have two cats, she [has] three. — the noun 'katten' and the verb 'heeft' are both elided.
examples.note_tr: Nominal + verbal ellipsis in a coordinated numeral contrast.

examples.target: Hoe meer, hoe beter.
examples.translation_tr: The more, the better. — both clauses omit the shared verb 'het is'.
examples.note_tr: Fixed correlative construction with obligatory ellipsis.

examples.target: Niet Jan komt, alleen Piet.
examples.translation_tr: It's not Jan who is coming, only Piet. — 'komt' is understood after 'alleen Piet'.
examples.note_tr: Corrective stripping contrasting two subjects.

nested-subclauses.intro_tr: In Dutch, subclauses can be embedded inside other subclauses, creating long chains where the finite verb (and any accompanying infinitives or participles) keeps getting pushed further toward the end of its own clause. Each layer of embedding (a dat-clause inside a dat-clause, a relative clause inserted mid-sentence, an omdat-clause tucked inside another subclause) adds distance between a word and the element it depends on — this is what linguists call a "long-distance dependency". Native speakers manage this with strict verb-cluster ordering rules, extraposition (moving heavy clauses to the end and leaving a dummy 'het'), and fronting strategies (wh-words, topicalized objects) that can "jump" across several clause boundaries. This page collects the core mechanics so you can both parse and produce these dense, layered sentences correctly.

tables.caption_tr: Anatomy of a Nested Clause Chain
Verb Cluster Order at the End of Multiple Embedded Clauses
rows: dat hij het boek gelezen heeft
dat hij het boek had willen lezen / willen lezen had
dat ze hem heeft horen zeggen / horen zeggen heeft
kunnen - doen - hebben - zou (avoided even in writing)
dat hij het zou hebben kunnen doen

tables.caption_tr: Conjunctions Frequently Stacked to Create Nested Subclauses
rows: Can be nested many layers deep: 'dat hij zegt dat ... dat ...'
Usually the innermost/final layer; rarely embeds further clauses itself
Often inserted mid-sentence, splitting subject and verb of the outer clause
Can be embedded inside a dat-clause to add a parenthetical contrast
Typically final in the chain, after the main content is established
Behaves like dat for word order; commonly embeds a relative clause
Frequently inserted directly after the noun it modifies, even mid-clause

tables.caption_tr: Long-Distance Dependencies: How Elements Cross Clause Boundaries
rows: A question word from an embedded clause moves to the front of the whole sentence
Wat denk je dat hij gezegd heeft?
The gap left behind is understood at the end of the embedded clause
When the extracted subject leaves its clause, 'er' fills the empty subject slot
Wie denk je dat er gebeld heeft?
Dropping 'er' here sounds ungrammatical to native ears
A heavy subject/object clause is moved to the end; dummy 'het' holds its place
Het verbaasde me dat hij te laat kwam.
Very common when the subclause is long or contains its own embedding
An object logically belonging to an inner clause is fronted in the outer one
Die vraag had ik niet verwacht dat hij zou stellen.
Creates a strong long-distance link between the fronted object and the deep verb
A relative clause is inserted directly after its antecedent, interrupting the main clause
De man die ik gisteren zag, werkt hier niet meer.
The main clause verb (werkt) is delayed until after the whole relative clause finishes

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Nested Subclauses
rows: Verb not moved to clause end
In every subclause the finite verb must go to the end, not stay in V2 position
dat hij had willen lezen (or: willen lezen had)
Only the fully red or fully green order is acceptable, not a random mix
Wie denk je dat gebeld heeft?
Wie denk je dat er gebeld heeft?
When the subject is questioned out of an embedded dat-clause, 'er' must appear
Forgetting extraposition, producing a heavy fronted subject
Dat hij, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam verbaasde me.
Het verbaasde me dat hij, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam.
Long subject clauses are normally extraposed with dummy 'het' rather than left in subject position
Losing track of which verb belongs to which clause in deep nesting
dat hij zegt dat hij komt morgen omdat hij vrij is dan
dat hij zegt dat hij morgen komt omdat hij dan vrij is
Each clause keeps its own adverbials and verb-final placement; they cannot bleed into the next clause

examples.target: Ik denk dat hij zegt dat hij morgen komt, omdat hij dan vrij is.
examples.translation_tr: I think that he says that he will come tomorrow, because he is free then.
examples.note_tr: Three clauses stacked: main clause + dat-clause + dat-clause + omdat-clause; each pushes the finite verb further to the end of its own clause.

examples.target: Ze wist niet of hij, die gisteren nog boos was, vandaag al vertrokken was.
examples.translation_tr: She didn't know whether he, who was still angry yesterday, had already left today.
examples.note_tr: A relative clause (die...was) is inserted inside an of-clause, splitting the subject from its verb by a long distance.

examples.target: Ik hoop dat je begrijpt dat ik, omdat ik ziek was, niet kon komen.
examples.translation_tr: I hope you understand that I, because I was sick, could not come.
examples.note_tr: An omdat-clause is embedded in the middle of a dat-clause, which is itself embedded in another dat-clause.

examples.target: Het verbaasde me dat hij, hoewel hij het druk had, toch tijd vond om te helpen.
examples.translation_tr: It surprised me that he, although he was busy, still found time to help.
examples.note_tr: Extraposition: the real subject (the dat-clause) is postponed and replaced by dummy 'het' in the main clause.

examples.target: Ze zei dat hij het boek had willen lezen.
examples.translation_tr: She said that he had wanted to read the book.
examples.note_tr: Three-verb cluster in red order (standard spoken/written Dutch): had - willen - lezen.

examples.target: Ze zei dat hij het boek willen lezen had.
examples.translation_tr: She said that he had wanted to read the book.
examples.note_tr: Same sentence in green order (more common in Belgian Dutch and formal/literary registers): willen - lezen - had.

examples.target: Wat denk je dat hij gisteren tegen haar gezegd heeft?
examples.translation_tr: What do you think he said to her yesterday?
examples.note_tr: Long-distance wh-dependency: 'wat' is the object of the embedded clause but is fronted all the way to the front of the main clause.

examples.target: Wie denk je dat er gisteren gebeld heeft?
examples.translation_tr: Who do you think called yesterday?
examples.note_tr: The subject 'wie' of the embedded clause is extracted to the main clause; 'er' appears as a placeholder subject in the subclause.

stylistic-inversion.title_tr: Stylistic Inversion and Heavy Element Shifting
stylistic-inversion.intro_tr: Dutch normally follows a strict verb-second (V2) word order, but formal, literary, and journalistic registers exploit two further devices for stylistic effect: stylistic inversion (placing the subject after the finite verb, or delaying it further than strictly required, even without any special trigger) and heavy element shifting / extraposition (moving long or syntactically complex constituents — subordinate clauses, relative clauses, prepositional complements — to the very end of the sentence, past material that would otherwise follow them). Both devices are governed by the same underlying principle of 'end-weight': informationally heavy, complex, or new material gravitates toward the right edge of the clause, while short, given, or pronominal material stays close to the verb. These constructions are frequent in narrative prose, news reports, and formal writing, but are much rarer in everyday spoken Dutch. Mastering them is essential for reading literature and formal texts fluently and for producing well-balanced, idiomatic written Dutch at an advanced level.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Stylistic Subject–Verb Inversion
rows: Standard in narrative dialogue; keeps focus on the speech act
Uit het donkere bos kwam, traag en dreigend, een grote wolf.
Builds suspense in literary narration by postponing the subject
Er wonen in dit dorp nog maar weinig oude vissersfamilies.
Introduces new, heavy referents at the end of the clause
Formal/journalistic register; news and legal reports
Nauwelijks was hij binnen, of de telefoon ging.

tables.caption_tr: Heavy Element Shifting (Extraposition) Patterns
rows: Het verbaasde iedereen [dat hij laat kwam].
Het verbaasde iedereen dat hij zo laat nog kwam.
Een man [die naar u vroeg] is langsgekomen.
Een man is langsgekomen [die naar u vroeg].
Er is gisteren een man langsgekomen die naar u vroeg.
PP-complement shifted past the final verb (subordinate clause)
...omdat hij gisteren heeft gesproken met de burgemeester van de stad.
Hij is [dan ik had gedacht] groter geworden.
Hij is groter geworden [dan ik had gedacht].
Hij is groter geworden dan ik ooit had gedacht.
Die buurman van ons is best aardig.
Hij is best aardig, [die buurman van ons].
Hij is toch wel aardig, die nieuwe buurman.

tables.caption_tr: Obligatory 'het' Placeholder When a Subject Clause Is Extraposed
rows: Het was duidelijk dat hij loog.
'Het' becomes obligatory once the clause is moved to the end
Om te winnen was zijn enige doel.
Het was zijn enige doel om te winnen.
Of hij zou komen, was onzeker.
Het was onzeker of hij zou komen.

tables.caption_tr: End-Weight Principle: Factors Favoring Rightward Shift
rows: Long or clause-like constituents move toward the end
...omdat hij besloten heeft te vertrekken naar een land waar niemand hem kent.
New information is placed late for emphasis
Er is nog iemand gearriveerd die we niet verwachtten.
Stays close to the verb, appearing early in the clause
Hij heeft het (= given) meteen gedaan.
Almost always extraposed rather than left in situ
Het is jammer dat je niet kon komen.
Never extraposed; always stay close to the verb
Ik heb het hem gisteren gegeven. (never: ...gegeven hem)

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes
rows: Dat hij laat kwam verbaasde iedereen.
Grammatically possible but stylistically clumsy; Dutch strongly prefers extraposition with 'het' for such clauses
Het verbaasde iedereen dat hij laat kwam.
...omdat hij heeft gesproken de burgemeester met.
A prepositional phrase can never be split across the sentence; it must move as one intact unit
...omdat hij heeft gesproken met de burgemeester.
Er een man is langsgekomen die naar u vroeg.
'Er' must be immediately followed by the finite verb; V2 order still applies inside stylistic constructions
Er is een man langsgekomen die naar u vroeg.
Het is duidelijk dat hij komt. (used for a very short, simple subject clause in casual speech)
Extraposition with 'het' is common but sounds overly formal for short, simple clauses in everyday conversation
Dat hij komt is duidelijk. (fine as a light, fronted clause in casual style)

examples.target: Er kwam, tot ieders verbazing, nog een late gast binnen.
examples.translation_tr: To everyone's surprise, one more late guest came in.
examples.note_tr: The heavy subject 'nog een late gast' is postponed past the parenthetical adverbial for dramatic effect.

examples.target: 'Dat kan toch niet waar zijn,' riep hij verontwaardigd uit.
examples.translation_tr: 'That surely can't be true,' he exclaimed indignantly.
examples.note_tr: Quotative inversion: verb-subject order after a direct quotation.

examples.target: Het is opvallend dat niemand hem op het feest heeft gezien.
examples.translation_tr: It's striking that nobody saw him at the party.
examples.note_tr: The dat-clause is extraposed to the end; 'het' fills the vacated subject position.

examples.target: Er is gisteren een brief gekomen die al drie weken onderweg was.
examples.translation_tr: A letter arrived yesterday that had been on its way for three weeks.
examples.note_tr: The relative clause is separated from its antecedent 'een brief' and shifted to clause-final position.

examples.target: Ik denk dat hij gisteren nog heeft gesproken met de burgemeester van de stad.
examples.translation_tr: I think he still talked yesterday with the mayor of the city.
examples.note_tr: The heavy PP 'met de burgemeester van de stad' is shifted past the final verb cluster of the subordinate clause.

examples.target: Nauwelijks was de storm gaan liggen, of het begon alweer te regenen.
examples.translation_tr: The storm had hardly died down when it started raining again.
examples.note_tr: Fronting of 'nauwelijks' triggers subject-verb inversion, typically followed by 'of'.

examples.target: Hij is toch wel aardig, die nieuwe buurman van ons.
examples.translation_tr: He's actually quite nice, that new neighbor of ours.
examples.note_tr: Right dislocation: the subject NP is repeated as an afterthought tag after the main clause.

examples.target: Aldus eindigde, na vele omzwervingen, het lange verhaal van de oude visser.
examples.translation_tr: Thus ended, after many wanderings, the long story of the old fisherman.
examples.note_tr: Literary fronting of 'aldus' with the heavy subject postponed to the very end.

dummy-subjects-advanced.intro_tr: In Dutch, both "het" and "er" can act as grammatical "dummy" (expletive) subjects — words that occupy the subject slot without referring to any real person or thing. The basic patterns are simple (weather "het regent", existential "er is een man"), but advanced, native-like Dutch requires knowing exactly when each dummy is obligatory, when "er" must be dropped because another element has taken the front (V2) position, and how "het" is used to anticipate a postponed dat-/of-clause. This page focuses on those advanced interactions: anticipatory "het" with clausal subjects, the obligatory deletion of existential/impersonal "er" once a locative or other adverbial is fronted, and the precise contrast between overlapping-looking "het" and "er" constructions that even advanced learners frequently confuse.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Dummy "het" (Impersonal het)
rows: Het is duidelijk dat hij liegt.
It is clear that he is lying.
Het wordt beweerd dat hij loog.
It is claimed that he lied.
She is doing well. (lit. 'it goes well with her')

tables.caption_tr: Dummy "er" vs. Dummy "het": How to Choose
rows: Introduces an indefinite, postponed real subject, or marks an impersonal passive with no subject
Fills the subject slot for weather/time/state, or anticipates a following dat-/of-clause
Is there a real subject somewhere?
Yes — an indefinite noun phrase postponed after the verb (or no subject at all in impersonal passive)
No real noun subject (weather/time), OR the real subject is the clause that follows
Er staat een man voor de deur.
Het staat vast dat hij komt.
Can it be dropped when another element is fronted?
Yes — often obligatorily dropped: 'Er wordt hier gewerkt' → 'Hier wordt gewerkt'
No — het can never simply be dropped; it can only move position (e.g. in questions: 'Regent het?')
Stays if still needed: '...dat er een man voor de deur staat.'
Stays and is obligatory: '...dat het vaststaat dat hij komt.'

tables.caption_tr: Extraposition Patterns: "het" Anticipating a Postponed Clause
rows: Het is vreemd dat hij niet belt.
It's strange that he doesn't call.
Het lijkt of het gaat regenen.
It seems like it's going to rain.
Het blijkt dat de brief nooit is aangekomen.
It turns out that the letter never arrived.
Het valt te betwijfelen of hij gelijk heeft.
It is doubtful whether he is right.
het + doet er niet toe + of-clause
Het doet er niet toe of je nu komt of later.
It doesn't matter whether you come now or later.
Het is de vraag of dit wel werkt.
The question is whether this even works.

tables.caption_tr: Deletion & Word-Order Rules for Dummy "er" (Advanced)
rows: Front position taken by an adverbial
Dummy er (impersonal passive placeholder) drops once 'hier' occupies the front (topic) position — Dutch normally does not allow both.
Front position taken by the real subject itself
Een probleem is er (rare/marked; usually avoided).
er normally stays because the real subject 'een probleem' is indefinite and stays postponed after the verb.
Word order after the complementizer is fixed (verb-final), so er stays where the existential subject still needs a placeholder.
Unlike existential er, dummy het for weather/time is a true grammatical subject and can only move (in questions/inversion), never disappear.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: het vs. er as Dummy Subject
rows: *Er is duidelijk dat hij gelijk heeft.
Het is duidelijk dat hij gelijk heeft.
Extraposition of a dat-/of-clause always uses het, never er.
*Het staat een man voor de deur.
Er staat een man voor de deur.
Existential 'there is/are' sentences require er, not het.
Once a locative adverbial like 'hier' is fronted, the impersonal-passive dummy er must be dropped, not doubled.
Is het duidelijk dat hij het weet?
In questions with inversion, dummy het moves after the finite verb but is never omitted.

examples.target: Het regent pijpenstelen.
examples.translation_tr: It's raining cats and dogs. (lit. 'it rains pipe-stems')
examples.note_tr: Idiomatic weather construction with obligatory dummy het.

examples.target: Het is duidelijk dat zij gelijk heeft.
examples.translation_tr: It is clear that she is right.
examples.note_tr: Anticipatory het introduces the postponed dat-clause, which is the real (logical) subject.

examples.target: Er staat een man voor de deur.
examples.translation_tr: There is a man standing at the door.
examples.note_tr: Existential er: the real, indefinite subject 'een man' is postponed after the verb.

examples.target: Hier wordt niet gerookt.
examples.translation_tr: No smoking (happens) here.
examples.note_tr: Compare to 'Er wordt hier niet gerookt.' — once 'hier' is fronted into first position, dummy er for the impersonal passive is dropped.

examples.target: Het valt te betwijfelen of hij op tijd komt.
examples.translation_tr: It is doubtful whether he'll arrive on time.
examples.note_tr: Fixed extraposition pattern 'het valt te betwijfelen of...' — het cannot be replaced by er here.

examples.target: Er schijnt een probleem te zijn met de auto.
examples.translation_tr: There appears to be a problem with the car.
examples.note_tr: Existential er combined with the semi-modal 'schijnen te' (to seem to).

examples.target: Het wordt beweerd dat hij loog.
examples.translation_tr: It is claimed that he lied.
examples.note_tr: Formal impersonal passive with anticipatory het introducing the dat-clause.

examples.target: Het doet er niet toe of je nu komt of later.
examples.translation_tr: It doesn't matter whether you come now or later.
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiom 'het doet er niet toe' contains both het (dummy subject) and the fossilized 'er' particle — do not confuse this 'er' with existential er.

nominal-style.intro_tr: "Ambtelijk taalgebruik" is the dense, noun-heavy register found in Dutch laws, official letters, reports, and government forms. Its defining feature is "nominalisering": actions and qualities that would normally be expressed by a verb or adjective are frozen into abstract nouns (typically with -ing, -atie, -heid, or "het + infinitive") and then reattached to the sentence via prepositions instead of conjugated verbs. This produces long, passive, agentless sentences built from formulaic prepositional phrases (met betrekking tot, ten aanzien van, naar aanleiding van) and "light verb + noun" collocations (een besluit nemen tot, in werking treden, overgaan tot) rather than plain active verbs. Although fully grammatical and associated with authority and precision, this style is explicitly discouraged by Dutch plain-language ("Klare Taal") guidelines for being needlessly opaque. At C2 level, learners should be able to both decode this register in official texts and consciously "unpack" it back into everyday, verb-driven Dutch.

examples.target: Ten aanzien van de ingediende aanvraag wordt overgegaan tot afwijzing.
examples.translation_tr: With regard to the submitted application, a rejection is proceeded to (i.e., it is rejected).
examples.note_tr: Plain equivalent: 'We wijzen de aanvraag af.' Note the formal preposition + passive light-verb construction replacing a simple active verb.

examples.target: De vaststelling van de nieuwe regeling geschiedt door de minister.
examples.translation_tr: The establishment of the new regulation is carried out by the minister.
examples.note_tr: Plain equivalent: 'De minister stelt de nieuwe regeling vast.' 'Geschieden' is an archaic formal verb meaning 'to occur/be done'.

examples.target: Met betrekking tot de uitvoering van het project dient men rekening te houden met de gestelde termijnen.
examples.translation_tr: With regard to the implementation of the project, one must take the set deadlines into account.
examples.note_tr: 'Dient men' (formal 'moet men') and the nominalized 'de uitvoering' both mark bureaucratic register.

examples.target: In verband met de sluiting van het gebouw wordt verzocht tijdig te vertrekken.
examples.translation_tr: In connection with the closing of the building, visitors are requested to leave in time.
examples.note_tr: Plain equivalent: 'Omdat we het gebouw sluiten, vragen we u op tijd te vertrekken.'

examples.target: Naar aanleiding van uw verzoek delen wij u het volgende mede.
examples.translation_tr: Further to your request, we hereby inform you of the following.
examples.note_tr: 'Mededelen' + formal connector is standard opening formula in official letters.

examples.target: Onderhavige regeling treedt in werking op de dag na de bekendmaking.
examples.translation_tr: The present regulation enters into force on the day after its publication.
examples.note_tr: 'Onderhavig(e)' = formal for 'deze/dit'; 'in werking treden' is a fixed light-verb collocation for 'to take effect'.

examples.target: Er wordt kennis genomen van de ingekomen stukken.
examples.translation_tr: Note is taken of the documents received.
examples.note_tr: Impersonal passive + light verb 'kennis nemen van' avoids naming an agent, typical of minutes/reports.

examples.target: Tot goedkeuring van het plan wordt besloten onder voorbehoud van nadere uitwerking.
examples.translation_tr: The plan is approved (lit. 'a decision to approval is made'), subject to further elaboration.
examples.note_tr: Double nominalization ('goedkeuring', 'uitwerking') stacked around a passive light verb 'besloten wordt tot' — dense C2-level bureaucratic syntax.

flemish-differences.title_tr: Belgian Flemish Differences (gij, ge, word choice)
flemish-differences.intro_tr: Belgian Dutch (Belgisch Nederlands / \"Flemish\") shares the same standard grammar as Netherlands Dutch but differs in several persistent features. Most famously, the archaic second-person pronouns \"gij\" (stressed) and \"ge\" (unstressed) are still fully alive in everyday Flemish speech and much informal writing, used where Netherlands Dutch would choose \"jij/je\", while \"u\" doubles as both the object form of \"gij\" and the polite form — so the informal/formal (T-V) split is much less sharp than in the Netherlands. Belgian Dutch also has its own vocabulary preferences, often shaped by French and regional dialects (e.g. \"goesting\", \"seffens\", \"schoon\"), and a handful of small grammatical quirks (like the imperative \"zijt\" instead of \"wees\"). This page is a practical reference for recognizing and using these Belgian features correctly, focused on the standard, widely accepted forms rather than deep dialect.

tables.caption_tr: Pronoun system: Standard Dutch (NL) vs. Belgian Flemish (BE)
rows: Gaat gij morgen mee? (addressing a group)
footnotes_tr: Because 'u' serves both as the object form of the informal 'gij' and as the formal pronoun, the informal/formal (T-V) distinction is far less sharp in Belgium than in the Netherlands.
'gullie' and 'gijlder' (plural 'gij') are dialectal and not used in standard written Belgian Dutch.
In careful written Standard Dutch as taught in Belgium, 'jij/je' are also understood and sometimes used, but 'gij/ge' remain fully acceptable and extremely common in speech and informal text.

tables.caption_tr: Full present-tense conjugation with gij/ge (compared to all persons)
footnotes_tr: Regular verbs simply keep the same -t ending with 'gij/ge' that Standard Dutch uses with 'jij/je' (e.g. 'werkt gij' = 'werk jij').
'zijn' is irregular: the form is always 'zijt' with 'gij/ge', never 'bent'.
Inversion in questions uses the same pattern as Standard Dutch: 'Hebt gij...?', 'Kunt ge...?', 'Zijt gij...?'.

tables.caption_tr: Common vocabulary differences: Netherlands Dutch (NL) vs. Belgian Flemish (BE)
footnotes_tr: 'schoon' is a classic false friend: in Netherlands Dutch it means 'clean', but in Belgian Dutch it primarily means 'beautiful/nice'.
Many Belgian words (goesting, content, allee, merci) trace back to French influence, reflecting Belgium's bilingual context.
Both sets of words are generally understood across the language area, but using the 'wrong' regional word can sound noticeably foreign or overly formal to a local audience.

tables.caption_tr: Other grammatical and stylistic features of Belgian Dutch
rows: 'Zijt' is used as the imperative form, replacing 'wees'.
manneke (little man), huiske (little house) — dialectal, not standard writing
Merci! Voilà, dat is gedaan. Amai, wat een chance!
Gij, gij zegt dat toch altijd zeker!
'k en weet het niet (dialectal; standard: ik weet het niet)
Preference for 'gaan' + infinitive over 'zullen' for near future
'gaan' strongly preferred even in fairly formal speech
Ik ga dat seffens doen. (rather than 'Ik zal dat zo doen.')
footnotes_tr: Diminutive forms in -ke/-eke and the negation particle 'en' belong to spoken dialect and informal registers; they are not used in standard formal Belgian Dutch writing.

Despite these differences, the written standard language (grammar, spelling, core vocabulary) taught in Belgian schools is the same 'Algemeen Nederlands' shared with the Netherlands — the features here concern register and regional usage, not a separate grammar.

examples.target: Gij zijt heel vriendelijk, hoor.
examples.translation_tr: You're very friendly, you know.
examples.note_tr: Belgian Flemish uses 'gij' as a neutral, everyday second-person singular pronoun where Netherlands Dutch would use 'jij'.

examples.target: Wat wilt gij drinken?
examples.translation_tr: What do you want to drink?
examples.note_tr: Regular verbs take the same -t ending with 'gij' as they do with 'jij' in Standard Dutch (wilt = wil je).

examples.target: Hebt ge dat al gezien?
examples.translation_tr: Have you seen that already?
examples.note_tr: 'ge' is the unstressed/clitic counterpart of 'gij', much like 'je' is the unstressed form of 'jij'.

examples.target: Ik ga seffens naar de winkel.
examples.translation_tr: I'll go to the shop in a moment.
examples.note_tr: 'seffens' is a common Belgian word for 'zo meteen/dadelijk' (in a moment), rarely used in the Netherlands.

examples.target: Awel, dat is een schoon kleedje!
examples.translation_tr: Well, that's a beautiful dress!
examples.note_tr: In Belgian Dutch 'schoon' usually means 'beautiful' (not 'clean'), and 'kleedje' is commonly used for 'jurk' (dress).

examples.target: Ik heb goesting in een pintje.
examples.translation_tr: I feel like having a beer.
examples.note_tr: 'goesting' (from French 'goût') is the standard Belgian word for 'zin' (craving/desire); 'pintje' is a casual word for a glass of beer.

examples.target: Kunt gij mij daarmee helpen?
examples.translation_tr: Can you help me with that?
examples.note_tr: Note 'kunt' with 'gij', parallel to 'kun jij' in Standard Dutch, not 'kan gij'.

examples.target: Zijt gerust, het komt wel goed.
examples.translation_tr: Don't worry, it will be fine.
examples.note_tr: 'Zijt' is also used as an imperative form of 'zijn' in Belgian Dutch ('Zijt gerust' = 'Wees gerust').

idiomatic-structures.intro_tr: Dutch idiomatic structures and proverbs (spreekwoorden en gezegdes) are fixed expressions whose internal grammar is frozen and cannot be reordered, inflected, or translated word-for-word. Many preserve archaic case endings, obsolete prepositions, and rigid word order that no longer exist anywhere else in modern Dutch grammar. Native speakers use these expressions constantly, so recognizing their fossilized structure — rather than trying to parse them with everyday rules — is essential for near-native comprehension. This page catalogs the main structural types of Dutch idioms, the most common proverbs, the archaic grammar trapped inside them, and the literal-translation traps learners typically fall into.
